Today, Lucene supports [8, 4, 2 and 1](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/e1879e450b75b3a58fde2b0dad77ae6b499504dd/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene104/Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsFormat.java#L119-L148) bit quantization.

Each quantization level typically has an upper bound of recall with exact KNN that it can produce (which is "exact KNN with quantized scores" v/s "exact KNN with original scores", see https://github.com/mikemccand/luceneutil/issues/528) -- this is the information loss due to quantization itself (before approximate-ness from search algorithms like HNSW comes into picture).

Any algorithm operating on quantized scores _alone_ cannot go beyond this recall (e.g. tweaking parameters like `maxConn`, `beamWidth`, `fanout`, etc. for HNSW) without using the original scores from un-quantized vectors for re-ranking -- which may not be feasible for some use cases (e.g. keeping the index in-memory for performance, where using un-quantized vectors increases memory footprint by \~4x in case of byte-quantized vectors).

### Description

Disclosure + Credit: I work at Amazon, and this idea was suggested by a colleague familiar with vector search (thanks Karthik!)

For quantized vector fields, HNSW graphs are initially built (during indexing) with [original (unquantized) vectors](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/98e1c075f709c13d501f91091e1b05f032279e48/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene99/Lucene99HnswVectorsWriter.java#L694-L699), but later (during merging) with [quantized vectors](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/98e1c075f709c13d501f91091e1b05f032279e48/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene99/Lucene99HnswVectorsWriter.java#L405-L406) (see [ref](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/98e1c075f709c13d501f91091e1b05f032279e48/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene104/Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsWriter.java#L568-L585)).

Would a graph built using original (unquantized) vectors every time (both indexing + merge) be higher quality, and better to search?

This is a tradeoff b/w increased indexing time (quantized computations are cheaper) v/s better recall + latency at search time.

### Description

Spinoff from #15836

A KNN query [short-circuits the HNSW search](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/83e3f9ac24ac282ae353d0e0566f64640fe919a3/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene99/Lucene99HnswVectorsReader.java#L345) if the "expected" number of nodes visited is >= number of filtered nodes.

A similarity-based vector query (i.e. `[Byte|Float]VectorSimilarityQuery`) attempts to find _all_ vectors with a score above a threshold (for Euclidean similarity, this can be imagined as all vectors within a radius of the query vector).

Assuming document vectors are evenly spread out across the n-dimensional space, should vector similarity scores form a normal distribution?

If so, can we estimate the proportion of nodes visited using area under the curve (from `resultSimilarity` -> `∞`) of a normal distribution? (and apply the same short circuit logic)

### Description

When Lucene90DocValuesConsumer writes a numeric doc values field, it iterates over the values multiple times - once to write skippers if they are configured, once to get minimum and maximum values for block encoding, once to write the values.  SortedNumeric repeats this, and then iterates again to write addresses if there are documents with multiple values.  Sorted and SortedSet re-use the numeric values machinery to write their ords, and SortedSet also adds in an iteration over all values to check to see if it can fall back to just Sorted.  BinaryDocValues iterates over everything to get minimum and maximum lengths before writing values out.

We should be able to use skipper metadata (where it exists) to avoid at least some of these multiple iterations, especially if we add more information such as maxValuesPerDoc.

## Description
Currently, the `KoreanTokenizer` in the Nori module segments numeric values containing decimal points into multiple separate tokens.

For example, the phrase **"10.1인치 모니터"** is currently tokenized as follows (when `discardPunctuation = false`):
`["10", ".", "1", "인치", "모니터"]`

**Why this is important (for example: Media/News Use Cases)**
In news datasets, numeric precision is vital for accurate information retrieval. Key values such as **economic growth rates ("3.5%"), poll results ("42.1%"), or exchange rates ("1532.26원")** are currently fragmented.

This leads to poor search relevancy for data-driven reporting, as it becomes difficult to search for specific numeric measurements or versions (e.g., searching for "10.1" might match "10" and "1" separately). Treating these as atomic units is essential for maintaining the semantic integrity of the data.

## Proposed Enhancement
I propose adding a new configuration option, `keepDecimalPoint` (boolean), to the `KoreanTokenizer`.

- Behavior: When set to `true`, the tokenizer treats a sequence of `[Digit][Dot][Digit]` as a single token during the lattice construction phase.
- Default value: `false` (to maintain backward compatibility).

## Example of desired output (`keepDecimalPoint=true`)
- Input: `"10.1인치 모니터"`
- Output: `["10.1", "인치", "모니터"]`

body_text:
### Description

After #15954, SortedNumericDocValuesRangeQuery uses SkipBlockRangeIterator as its two-phase approximation. I see that `SkipBlockRangeIterator.cost()` currently returns `NO_MORE_DOCS`, which means when multiple DV range queries are combined in a FILTER conjunction, both DenseConjunctionBulkScorer and ConjunctionDISI will sort the clauses in arbitrary order as they all report the same cost?

I wonder if we should have a better way to do this. That is, we choose the most selective field(the one which can eliminate most docs) as the lead iterator, as this will allow us to skip most of the docs. This might help in performance depending on the number of fields in range conjunctions, higher the no. of fields, better ordering will give better performance.

The DocValuesSkipper already has metadata that could help estimate selectivity ie global minValue()/maxValue(), per-block min/max, and docCount(). Some ideas to do this:

 - Use skipper.docCount() as cost. Though only differentiate b/w sparse vs dense fields.
 - Estimate selectivity from queryRange / fieldRange * docCount.  Rough but differentiates narrow vs wide queries
 - Count NO blocks by walking the skip tree at scorer creation. This is more accurate, O(num_blocks) but requires extra work ahead.

body_text:
### Description

This class exposes a bunch of new capabilities, but they aren't adequately documented.  In order to make use of the skipper, you need a mental model of the skip list data structure and the implicit assumptions that are being made by this class.  Some things I found out that weren't clear at first:

1. Level 0 is the "top" level with the largest blocks; higher numbered levels represent successively nested sub-blocks.
2. The skipper only really works with fields that are primary index sort keys (I think?). What happens if you try to use the skipper with non-sorted fields? Can you still read block level statistics? Maybe - but how does skipping function in that case?
3. advance(docId) is forward-only, but what are the expectations around `advance(minValue, maxValue)`? Is it possible to reverse using this API?

I can try to improve the docs, but my understanding is only superficial, and I don't want to add to the confusion, so for now I'm just asking questions :)

body_text:
I am working into improving the behaviour of DocValues skippers when they are applied to a single value, dense field that is the primary sort of an index. In this case, for some queries we know the result is dense so we can just find the minimum and maximum document of the result and create a DocIdSetIterator using `DocIdSetIterator.range(minDocID, maxDocID)`. This is the denser representation you can have for this type of iterator.

The issue I am seeing is that if this iterator get cached it looses the density and potentially can be cached as a FixedBitSet. This feels pretty wasteful and in addition it looses some characteristics, for example if cached as a RoaringDocIdSet, then the iterator produced does not implement #docIdRunEnd so you need to iterate one document at a time.

I cannot see a way to detect a scorer is dense so I wonder if someone has suggestions on how to improve this case. Maybe we should not cache such queries although caching still helps here.

In concurrent search with timeout in IndexSearcher, when a timeout happens, one slice hits it but still continues processing remaining leaves and keeps failing repeatedly.

Other slices also continue running until they hit the timeout on their own.

This leads to some unnecessary extra work after the timeout.

Would it make sense to stop all slices immediately once any one slice hits the timeout?

experimental columnar indexing API (`IndexWriter.addBatch(ColumnBatch)`) added supports bulk columnar document addition, but there is no equivalent to `updateDocuments(Term, Iterable)` 
for columnar batches. Users who index via columns cannot atomically delete existing documents by term 
and add a new columnar batch in a single operation.

add the following public methods to `IndexWriter`

```java
/**
 * Atomically deletes documents matching the provided term and adds a batch of documents 
 * in column-oriented format.
 */
public long updateDocuments(Term delTerm, ColumnBatch columnBatch) throws IOException;

/**
 * Similar to above but takes a Query instead of a Term.
 */
public long updateDocuments(Query delQuery, ColumnBatch columnBatch) throws IOException;

### Description

`IBSimilarity` with `DistributionSPL` can produce negative scores for very large tf values, which `TestSynonymQuery.testBoosts()` uses.  We don't have a good way to suppress individual Similarity implementations for tests at the moment, but I think in any case we should be looking to fix the root Similarity itself?  Impacts and competitive iterators all assume that scores can't be negative, a contract which this Similarity breaks.

### Gradle command to reproduce

On `branch_10x`:
```
./gradlew :lucene:core:test --tests "org.apache.lucene.search.TestSynonymQuery.testBoosts" -Ptests.jvms=12 -Ptests.jvmargs= -Ptests.seed=EC3CC718CF767FE7 -Ptests.useSecurityManager=false -Ptests.gui=true
  -Ptests.file.encoding=US-ASCII -Ptests.vectorsize=default -Ptests.forceintegervectors=false
```

body_text:
### Description

**Summary**

Since 10.0, an unanchored MultiTermQuery — a leading wildcard like `*foo*`, or a leading-.* regexp — used as a FILTER/MUST clause in a BooleanQuery can be dramatically slower than in 9x, even when the overall query matches zero documents.

The cause is that the term-dictionary scan for these queries moved from a lazy step (`ScorerSupplier#get()`) to an eager one (`Weight#scorerSupplier()`). `scorerSupplier()` is meant to be the cheap "planning" phase, and doing the scan there defeats a parent conjunction's ability to short-circuit before the scan runs.


**Root cause**

`AbstractMultiTermQueryConstantScoreWrapper#scorerSupplier()` now calls `collectTerms()` eagerly (to compute an accurate cost and to return null when no terms match, so a parent BooleanQuery can short-circuit). For a query with an unknown term count (any automaton query — `getTermsCount() == -1`), collectTerms walks the field's term dictionary, and a leading wildcard can't seek, so it must visit every term. The worst case is when it matches few/no terms and never reach the 16-term threshold, it scans the entire term dictionary.

Because BooleanWeight builds a ScorerSupplier for every clause up front, this scan runs before the conjunction can discover that a sibling required clause matches nothing. In 9 the scan lived in `get()`, so an empty sibling short-circuited the conjunction and the wildcard's get() was never called.

**Performance analysis**
From local benchmarking
| scenario | 9.11.1 | 10.1.0 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Build the `ScorerSupplier` only (no scorer built yet) | ~0.01 ms | ~41 ms | **~4000× slower** |
| `FILTER(*foo*) AND FILTER(<term that matches 0 docs>)` → 0 hits | ~0.15 ms | ~53 ms | **~350× slower** |
| Wildcard scorer actually built (`ScorerSupplier#get()`), nothing skips it | ~40 ms | ~50 ms | ~unchanged |

**Potential fixes (Open for discussion)**
1. Defer collectTerms to get() when term count is unknown https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/16222. We'll keep the eager path only for known, bounded term sets. The trade-off here is it reverts some of the cost estimation improvements brought by #13201.
2. A more targeted "is this automaton seekable/anchored?" signal so anchored automaton queries keep precise cost and only truly-unanchored ones defer. Cleaner in principle, but there's no obvious cheap signal (a non-empty common prefix doesn't guarantee a cheap scan).
3. Bound the eager scan effort and fall back to lazy? This sounds over complicated.

**Summary**

Since 10.0, an unanchored MultiTermQuery — a leading wildcard like `*foo*`, or a leading-.* regexp — used as a FILTER/MUST clause in a BooleanQuery can be dramatically slower than in 9x, even when the overall query matches zero documents.

The cause is that the term-dictionary scan for these queries moved from a lazy step (`ScorerSupplier#get()`) to an eager one (`Weight#scorerSupplier()`). `scorerSupplier()` is meant to be the cheap "planning" phase, and doing the scan there defeats a parent conjunction's ability to short-circuit before the scan runs.


**Root cause**

`AbstractMultiTermQueryConstantScoreWrapper#scorerSupplier()` now calls `collectTerms()` eagerly (to compute an accurate cost and to return null when no terms match, so a parent BooleanQuery can short-circuit). For a query with an unknown term count (any automaton query — `getTermsCount() == -1`), collectTerms walks the field's term dictionary, and a leading wildcard can't seek, so it must visit every term. The worst case is when it matches few/no terms and never reach the 16-term threshold, it scans the entire term dictionary.

Because BooleanWeight builds a ScorerSupplier for every clause up front, this scan runs before the conjunction can discover that a sibling required clause matches nothing. In 9 the scan lived in `get()`, so an empty sibling short-circuited the conjunction and the wildcard's get() was never called.

**Performance analysis**
From local benchmarking
| scenario | 9.11.1 | 10.1.0 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Build the `ScorerSupplier` only (no scorer built yet) | ~0.01 ms | ~41 ms | **~4000× slower** |
| `FILTER(*foo*) AND FILTER(<term that matches 0 docs>)` → 0 hits | ~0.15 ms | ~53 ms | **~350× slower** |
| Wildcard scorer actually built (`ScorerSupplier#get()`), nothing skips it | ~40 ms | ~50 ms | ~unchanged |

**Potential fixes (Open for discussion)**
1. Defer collectTerms to get() when term count is unknown https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/16222. We'll keep the eager path only for known, bounded term sets. The trade-off here is it reverts some of the cost estimation improvements brought by #13201.
2. A more targeted "is this automaton seekable/anchored?" signal so anchored automaton queries keep precise cost and only truly-unanchored ones defer. Cleaner in principle, but there's no obvious cheap signal (a non-empty common prefix doesn't guarantee a cheap scan).
3. Bound the eager scan effort and fall back to lazy? This sounds over complicated.

KoreanTokenizer expects precomposed Hangul syllables. When the same Korean text is supplied in NFD form, modern Hangul syllables become conjoining jamo sequences and Nori falls back to UNKNOWN eojeol-sized tokens instead of dictionary morphemes.

Minimal repro on current main: NFC "한국어 형태소를 분석합니다" produces 한국어/한국/어/형태소/형태/소/를/분석/합니다/하/ᄇ니다. NFD of the same text produces UNKNOWN tokens for each whitespace-delimited Korean span — so NFD-sourced text indexed beside NFC Korean text is silently unfindable.

This input shape is common in the wild: it is the same NFD text Korean users see as "jamo-separated" filenames when macOS-created archives are opened elsewhere. The same bytes reach indexes through filenames, extracted document text, and metadata pipelines.

Proposed fix: an opt-in analysis-nori CharFilter that composes only modern Hangul conjoining jamo sequences (L U+1100..U+1112, V U+1161..U+1175, optional T U+11A8..U+11C2) into precomposed syllables before KoreanTokenizer, with offset correction back to the original input. It is deliberately narrower than NFC: a precomposed LV syllable followed by a trailing jamo is left unchanged (that shape does not occur in NFD output). For general Unicode normalization the ICU module's ICUNormalizer2CharFilter remains the right tool; this covers the common Korean-only case without adding the ICU dependency to nori deployments.

## Background I am looking at the `ByteBlockPool` sharing design in `TermsHash` (related to #11608). Today, `TermsHash` uses a single shared `ByteBlockPool` to store both term bytes (used by `BytesRefHash`) and terms' postings data (doc ID deltas, freqs, pos, offsets, payloads). 16 years ago, in the initial [commit](https://github.com/apache/lucene/commit/42b9f0caa32ff71782a949264d033a346ede7b26#diff-22ab6c31dc6317827019d7c86faa08fc826efe921188da71743bc3b884d058ee), the `termBytePool` has been pointed to the same object as `bytePool`: ```java // In TermsHash constructor if (nextTermsHash != null) { termBytePool = bytePool; // reuse the same pool here nextTermsHash.termBytePool = bytePool; } ``` This means term bytes and their respective postings slices are interleaved in the same byte pool. I drew a diagram to illustrate: ![pool-sharing-diagram](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/40c19ae8-87ea-4b94-ac72-48ef464c3996) ## The Change and Benchmark Separating the two pools is simple (see my [commit](https://github.com/apache/lucene/commit/8138180422371fe9f24b6171985de749aa4d2543)) with just a few lines of code. I ran both micro and end-to-end benchmarks to vet. All benchmarks run on EC2 c5.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32G RAM), OpenJDK 25.0.2. ### JMH Microbenchmark I wrote a JMH benchmark that runs `TermsHashPerField.add()` in a tight loop for a single field, see the benchmark [here](https://github.com/apache/lucene/commit/58c86c4326d36482fc0fcc37a639b4ce6c0466fe). It uses 256k vocab size, 2M token stream with different Zipfian-ish skew configs, and a UUID unique workload, 1k tokens per doc. The Zipfian-ish skew way simulates the frequent seen terms in real workloads as I observed in https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/11608#issuecomment-5265355538. Two microbenchmarks: `indexSegment` (add only) and `indexSegmentAndSort` (add + radix sort, mimic the in-memory accumulation phase before segment flush). The UUID microbenchmark case (all unique) is neutral, an disabling the body field in end-to-end is also neutral, so without heavy inverted-index work, there is not much term-hash cache pressure to optimize and UUID benefits most from denser terms sort. ## Asks and guidance required I remember @rmuir once expressed in https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/16371#issuecomment-5053592144 that "It might look good in a microbenchmark but not in an overall indexer run.". My findings are the opposite, the microbenchmark shows no gain (or slight cost from the extra indirection), but the end-to-end indexer run shows a consistent improvement or no regression. So I'd like to seek guidance from experts and folks who are familiar with this area to help justify whether such separation is worth shipping. Happy to discuss. ### Description

In the OSQ based vector format, we [recalculate centroids on merge](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/bc9adc96cc58d1e20761d961a2ab865eaede3962/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene104/Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsWriter.java#L471) when there are deletes.
If there [aren't any deletes](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/bc9adc96cc58d1e20761d961a2ab865eaede3962/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene104/Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsWriter.java#L465), the merged centroid is simply a weighted average of segment-level centroids.

I wonder if we can re-use the information of the previous centroid, even when there are deletes?
i.e. start with `previousCentroid * vectorCount`, and _subtract deleted vectors_ instead?

If the number of deletes is small, perhaps the work is much lesser? The caveat is that vectors may be read at non-contiguous parts of the raw vector file if we just read deleted ones.

This can be especially beneficial for cases where raw vectors go beyond RAM, by avoiding some paging activity?

Going one step further: the access pattern could be improved further if the raw format was more tightly integrated. Currently we perform three passes over the raw vectors:
1. [Merge raw vectors](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/bc9adc96cc58d1e20761d961a2ab865eaede3962/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene104/Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsWriter.java#L327)
2. [Compute the centroid](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/bc9adc96cc58d1e20761d961a2ab865eaede3962/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene104/Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsWriter.java#L483-L504)
3. [Perform scalar quantization](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/bc9adc96cc58d1e20761d961a2ab865eaede3962/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene104/Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsWriter.java#L391-L394)

Can we compute the centroid in (1) and use it directly in (3), skipping (2)?

### Description

I noticed this while investigating an index under sustained updates where deleted documents accumulated without being reclaimed.

`LogMergePolicy.findMerges` can leave heavily deleted segments unmerged when their level has too few segments to form a merge. New segments may reach a level too slowly to keep up with accumulated deletes, even under continued indexing.

The policy requires `mergeFactor` segments to form an initial candidate, but may merge fewer of them to stay within the size limit.

`calibrateSizeByDeletes` scales estimated segment sizes by `(1 - delRatio)`. This can change level grouping and make previously oversized candidates eligible. Deletes therefore can trigger a merge indirectly through size-based selection, but there is no separate trigger based on the amount of reclaimable deletes.

#### Behavior

Selection tests using stock Lucene defaults. Each cell indicates whether a merge was selected.

**LogByteSizeMergePolicy** (`mergeFactor=10`, `maxMergeMB=2048`, `minMergeMB=16`):

| Segments | 0% deleted | 20% | 30% | 50% | 99% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2, 6, or 9 | No | No | No | No | No |
| 10 or 64 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

**TieredMergePolicy** (`segmentsPerTier=8`, `maxMergedSegmentMB=5120`, `deletesPctAllowed=20`):

| Segments | 0% deleted | 20% | 30% | 50% | 99% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2, 6, or 9 | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| 10 or 64 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Reading across each row, `LogByteSizeMergePolicy` gives the same answer at every tested delete fraction in this setup. `TieredMergePolicy` changes its answer with the delete fraction alone.

**With nine segments at 99% deletes, `LogByteSizeMergePolicy` selects nothing; `TieredMergePolicy` selects a merge.** `TieredMergePolicy` uses its index-wide deletion budget, selecting merges at the first tested percentage above `deletesPctAllowed=20`.

I'll push a companion PR with a couple of tests that reproduce this behavior and link it here.

#### Reclamation latency

As a simplified illustration, with 50 MB flush segments and full `mergeFactor = f` merges, segment size at level `k` is `50 MB × f^k`. Producing `f` such segments requires `f^(k+1)` flushes:

| Level | Segment size | Full level size | Flushes required | Flushes (f = 10) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 50 MB | 500 MB | f | 10 |
| 1 | 500 MB | 5 GB | f² | 100 |
| 2 | 5 GB | 50 GB | f³ | 1,000 |

This assumes no size reduction from deletes or compression changes and a sufficiently large maximum merge size. The default 2048 MB limit already truncates merges of the 500 MB segments at level 1.

At a constant flush rate, higher levels take geometrically longer to fill and can hold tens of gigabytes while still below the segment-count threshold. Deletes left unreclaimed during that wait inflate storage relative to live data, increasing production storage requirements and costs; the exact recoverable bytes depend on the data and codec.

#### Discussion

[#905](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/905) already established a delete-reclamation exception to `TieredMergePolicy`'s anti-thrashing rule. That policy also allows singleton merges that reclaim deletes. Should the same principle apply to `LogMergePolicy`?

Two possible approaches are:

- **Smaller adjacent merges:** allow fewer than `mergeFactor` segments when a level holds substantial reclaimable data.
- **Singleton rewrites:** allow individual delete-heavy segments to be rewritten.

Both preserve adjacency and trade additional write amplification for shorter reclamation latency. 

Related: [#13226](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/13226) reports similar symptoms under `TieredMergePolicy`, though the cause may differ.

body_text:
### Description

We have been adding FP16 support at various places in Lucene. Listing them below:

* Add fp16 (float16) vector encoding support, no quantization support: #16383
* Add scalar quantization support for Fp16 vector encoding: #16473 
* Fp16 re ranking and prefetch support: #16628 (Still not reviewed and merged)

I think there are few more places where the Fp16 support is still missing from the main branch. This is an overview issue which tracks all the task where we need to add the support. Listing few tasks below which I am able to identify but there might be more:

- [x] `DiversifyingChildrenFloat16KnnVectorQuery` (lucene/join). Parent-block-join diversifying KNN. `Float` and `Byte` siblings exist; no fp16 variant.
- [x] `Float16VectorSimilarityQuery` (lucene/core). Threshold based vector search. `FloatVectorSimilarityQuery` and `ByteVectorSimilarityQuery` exist over `AbstractVectorSimilarityQuery` but no fp16 subclass.
- [x] Implement scalar quantization support for FP16 vectors in newly added de-duplicating vector format (Also being tracked as part of #16595)
- [ ] `PanamaVectorUtilSupport`. `short[]` dotProduct/cosine/squareDistance currently delegate to the scalar implementation (`FLOAT16_DELEGATE`). SIMD vectorization is not possible today; it depends on a future JDK release adding `Float16Vector` support.
- [ ] In Faiss codec.

There could be more, so please feel free to add more tasks here.

Hi all,

I've been reading through the HNSW construction path (HnswGraphBuilder, OnHeapHnswGraph, NeighborArray, InitializedHnswGraphBuilder) and found something I couldn't explain from the code, so I'd like to check whether it's deliberate.

[InitializedHnswGraphBuilder.rebalanceGraph()](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/e357029271b3de560a6ff13c9cab4d4c8103b53b/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/util/hnsw/InitializedHnswGraphBuilder.java#L429) creates its own random source with no seed:

```java
private void rebalanceGraph() throws IOException {
  SplittableRandom random = new SplittableRandom();   // no seed
  ...
      if (random.nextDouble() < invMaxConn && !hnsw.nodeExistAtLevel(level, node)) {
        hnsw.addNode(level, node);
```

This decides which nodes get promoted to upper levels after a merge. Everywhere else on this path the randomness is threaded deliberately:

HnswGraphBuilder takes a seed, and its javadoc says "Provide this to ensure repeatable construction"
getRandomGraphLevel(ml, random) uses that seeded instance
HnswConcurrentMergeBuilder passes HnswGraphBuilder.randSeed to each worker
HnswGraphTestCase.testRandomReadWriteAndMerge explicitly sets HnswGraphBuilder.randSeed = seed before exercising merges with deletes

Since #15003, the repair/rebalance path only runs when the segment has deletes. testRandomReadWriteAndMerge does randomly delete documents, so as far as I can tell it reaches this path — but the promotion decisions inside rebalanceGraph() don't use randSeed, so re-running with the same seed would not reproduce the same level structure.

This doesn't show up as flakiness today, because the tests that exercise merge-with-deletes assert fairly shallow properties — testRandomReadWriteAndMerge asserts that the vector dimension survived, and testGraphMergeWithDeletes asserts the live node count. BaseIndexFileFormatTestCase.testMergeStability, which does compare merged output, indexes and force-merges without deletions, so it doesn't reach this path at all.

So the concern isn't a failing test — it's that if something does go wrong on this path (which was raised as the main testing concern during review of #15003), the seed wouldn't fully reproduce it.

Two questions:

Is the unseeded random intentional — e.g. because rebalancing is a heuristic whose exact outcome isn't meant to be reproducible?
If not, would it make sense to thread the builder's seed (or HnswGraphBuilder.randSeed) through to this method? I'd be glad to put up a patch.

I may be missing context — if the seeding choice was discussed somewhere, a pointer would be welcome.

Thanks,
Xin Zhang

body_text:
### Description

[Spinoff from [this comment](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/15979#discussion_r4168808020)]

Not sure if this is a silly idea or might be helpful:

We have painful cases today where the same mapped file sometimes should be optimized with `MADV_RANDOM`, say when reading full precision vectors for re-ranking in a `VectorQuery`, or sometimes with `MADV_SEQUENTIAL`, say when merging.  The hint is surprisingly impactful!  I've seen benchmarks take many minutes (when it should've been a few seconds) on a fast-ish NVMe SSD because the vector files were hinted the wrong way.

We have fragile logic that will flip the hint of the same mapped region to `SEQUENTIAL` when a merge is running, then back to `RANDOM` when the merge is done.

But couldn't we just map the same file twice, so we don't have to toggle the hinting?  The kernel will still load the pages once from file and share them across both (or more than two) maps.  Claude Opus 5.5 Medium [seems to think modern Linux kernels would do the right thing](https://claude.ai/share/e3c1b5ea-a22e-42b1-ab26-44fdf22c91eb) as long as we also `open(...)` the file twice (two file descriptors) -- i.e. the hints would stay separate.  But maybe it's optimistically hallucinating for me...

There would be an added cost of minor page faults for the kernel to share a single cached page in the buffer cache for both maps.  I.e. if a page became hot because of readahead from the merging, when a query then needs that page, there is a minor page fault to do the accounting so that the `RANDOM` map shares that same hot page.

### Description

As of today, when one index a double field(prices, coordinates etc) as doc values, lucene often stores it essentially uncompressed ie around 8 bytes per value. That's because doubles are converted to a long via `NumericUtils.doubleToSortableLong` before storage, so sorting and range queries work as plain long comparisons. But the numeric doc values encoders (GCD, FOR, etc.) don't work well on them, the decimal structure of the values is lost in the IEEE-754 bit pattern, so there's little left for these integer techniques to exploit. 

While reading about ALP (Adaptive Lossless floating-Point, SIGMOD 2024), seems like it uses a clever technique. For a block of values(1024), it picks an exponent e and encodes each digit as = `round (value * 10^e)`, so 90.11 becomes 9011, then apply FOR(Frame of reference) and other techniques, and bit pack smaller integers. Decode is just `value = digit / 10^e`. Any rare high-precision outlier is recorded as an exception (position, original) and patched back on read, so it's bit-exact lossless regardless of the data.

For columns that genuinely are high precision (scientific doubles like 23.718281828459045 etc) the `×10^e` trick can't produce small integers, so there's a second scheme which is tried i.e. ALP_RD: split each value's bits into a high part (low cardinality -> dictionary-encoded) and a low part (random -> stored raw). It's a smaller win (~1.1–1.2×) but still helps. And its adaptive per block like how we also classify our blocks into sparse/dense in lucene.

I did some experimentation and saw up to 3x savings in storage for doubles with few decimal places, like prices with 2 decimal places (e.g. 437.29), going from ~64 to ~20 bits per value. 

I think if we have to do this, best way would be put into this sandbox module as a experimental feature, by defining custom ALP codecs. We can probably use our existing docValuesSkipper built on top of this and reuse it on the search side.

### Description

## Problem

In document-oriented vector search, multiple documents frequently carry identical embeddings. Today `Lucene99HnswVectorsFormat` assigns each duplicate vector its own graph node rather than merging or otherwise accounting for them. When duplicates are skewed (Zipf-distributed in my case), the hot copies form a  sort of a sink where many edges point into the group, but the group has very few outgoing level-0 edges (only from selective nodes) to any other distinct-vector neighborhood.

When the graph's single entry point happens to land inside or adjacent to such a sink, the greedy level-0 search descends into it and dead-ends after visiting only a few dozen nodes. The result in a pretty dramatic recall collapse as shown below.

## Evidence

### Dataset generation

I generated the dataset in two ways:

1. **Uniform duplication:** every one of the 1,000 distinct vectors is repeated exactly 10 times to reach 10,000 documents, so no vector is more common than any other.
2. **Skewed (Zipf) duplication:** the repeat counts follow a Zipf distribution (exponent s = 1.0): a few vectors are copied an large number of times — the hottest one appears in 1,336 of the 10,000 documents — while a long tail of vectors appears only once or a handful of times.

Both datasets drew from the same 1,000 distinct source vectors; they differ only in how the duplicates are distributed.

### Recall Metrics

To correctly identify the behaviour of the graph, I defined two different forms of recall. 

- Distinct Recall@10 — Returned docs (rank order) are mapped back to the distinct vector they carry, deduplicated, and the first 10 distinct vectors are compared against ground truth (the 10 closest distinct embeddings, brute-forced over the 1,000 unique vectors). I collect 500 results here and then run the distinct check. 
- Tie-aware Document Recall@10 — Of the 10 highest-ranked docs, how many are legitimately in the exact top-10? Since identical vectors score identically, a doc is credited when its score ≥ the exact 10th-place score. This avoids penalizing a "different but equally-correct" duplicate.

### Results

The two data-sets behaved very differently:

1. With uniform duplication, distinct Recall@10 stayed near-perfect, averaging about 0.99 (0.9899 at maxConn 16 and 0.9921 at maxConn 32), and it was extremely stable — across all ten builds it stayed within a tight 0.9886–0.9934 range.
2. With skewed (Zipf) duplication, distinct Recall@10 collapsed to roughly 0.29–0.41 on average (mean 0.4082 at maxConn 16 and 0.2913 at maxConn 32) and swung wildly from build to build (individual builds ranged from 0.0073 to 0.6325).

| Workload | Distinct R@10 | Document R@10 (tie-aware) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deduplicated | 1.0000 ± 0.0000 | 1.0000 ± 0.0000 |
| Uniform duplicates | 0.9899 ± 0.0015 | 0.9973 ± 0.0006 |
| **Skewed duplicates** | **0.4082 ± 0.2416** | **0.3089 ± 0.1921** |
| All-unique (ref) | 1.0000 ± 0.0001 | 1.0000 ± 0.0001 |



### Possible Explanation?

My hunch is that when many identical vectors are indexed, Lucene gives each one its own graph node — it does not merge them into a shared node. Because all these copies sit at distance zero from one another, the resulting structure is a **largely isolated subgraph with hub-and-spoke connectivity.** In one of the build which I tried inspecting, most of the hot group's level-0 outgoing edges all remain within the duplicate group, leaving very few directed level-0 path from those nodes to any distinct-vector group.

### Description

As part of doing a new major version we should also consider deprecating parts of the codebase that are unmaintained or block further development, to be removed in the unstable branch once we have forked for version 11.

We had a discussion at Community over Code 2026 and came up with the following suggestions.  Let's discuss in this issue.

### Span Queries

SpanQueries have some basically unfixable correctness bugs and in any case have been superseded by IntervalQueries.  We should deprecate them, and produce instructions on how to migrate to Intervals.

### ValueSource

ValueSource provides per-document values via a random access API, which does not fit with the rest of lucene's iterator-based APIs and can be very trappy performance-wise.  We already have DoubleDocValues and LongDocValues to handle numeric values via iterators.  Let's deprecate ValueSource and see if we need to add any other iterator-based values to replace it.

### Highlighters

We have four highlighters, and it is not at all obvious which one to pick for new users.  Let's deprecate the classic and fast-vector highlighters and push users towards the unified highlighter, or the matches highlighter components if they need something more bespoke.

### Query parsers

We have seven (!) query parsers, most of which have not seen any updates for many years.  People who need complex parsers beyond what classic and simple offer are going to be rolling their own, or extending QueryParserBase from classic.  The XML query parser is mainly a source of security issues.  Let's deprecate xml, ext, complexPhrase, surround and flexible.

Today a merged segment warmer (`IndexWriter.IndexReaderWarmer` set using `IndexWriterConfig#setMergedSegmentWarmer`) runs synchronously on the merge thread, right before the writer publishes the new segment. The merge thread stays blocked for the whole duration of warming.

I use a warmer very much like the one in the replicator package (`PreCopyMergedSegmentWarmer`): it opens a reader on the freshly merged segment and does real work on it before that segment becomes visible. In my case warming isn't cheap and while it runs the merge thread is pinned doing no merge related work. So other pending merges queue up behind it even though the heavy `mergeMiddle` work for that merge is already done.

I'd like to propose making warming optionally asynchronous. The merge thread would finish writing the merge, hand the warming off, and immediately be free to pick up the next merge. Warming would happen in the background; the merged segment simply wouldn't be published until the warming completes. The default can stay synchronous so nothing changes unless you opt in.

I think it's worth it: the merge threads are released as soon as the merge is written so warming no longer inteferes with merges throughput. The warming cost (loading structures, pre-copying to replicas, whatever the warmer does) is removed off the critical merge path.

Anecdotally, this would also compound better with something like #16571 (letting a single merge write more than one output segment) since more outputs per merge means more readers to warm per merge, so keeping warming off the merge thread matters even more there.

I gave it a try in #16846 for those who would like to see how it could look. 

The exception handling is the hard part because once warming runs in the background there's no caller left to rethrow to. But it turned out less messy than I expected, mostly because warming happens at the very end after the bulk of the merge work is already done and on disk. I think the publish/commit step can simply run on the warmer thread once warming succeeds. And since a merge that's still warming is kept in the IndexWriter's "running" set the shutdown semantics seem to hold up (ie,  waitForMerges()/close()/rollback() would already block until warming is done).

body_text:
### Description

Follow-up from #16674 , @mikemccand [pointed out](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/16674#issuecomment-6018767712) that  [checkIntegrity](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/8476457b8752be2fd8094eaf5cd9bf0cea9594ae/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/KnnVectorsWriter.java#L123-L131) does another full read of `.vec` before [raw copy](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/8476457b8752be2fd8094eaf5cd9bf0cea9594ae/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene99/Lucene99FlatVectorsWriter.java#L300-L331), and that it is nearly redundant, since steps 1-2 could verify the checksum while they read.
The PR #16839 contribute to remove centroid pass[step 2], we need dig into if we have chance to simplify checkIntegrity as step 0. Here are proposal changes:

- Add a merge-specific check to `KnnVectorsReader`, the existing merge argument only makes the [check abortable](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/8476457b8752be2fd8094eaf5cd9bf0cea9594ae/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/CodecUtil.java#L654), so it can't be reused to mean 'skip'.
- The flat reader overrides it: while the merge reads `.vec`, it also computes the file's checksum from start to end , reading any bytes the merge skips(for example: deleted vectors), and compares it with the footer at the end.
- If the merge does not read in file order, fall back to the full check.
- No check `.veq` during merges. since step 3 recomputes it from `.vec`.  We will keep the full check for `.vex`. 

```text
Reads of the source files in one merge, for segments with deletes

              step 0           step 1                     step 2     step 3        .vec reads
              checkIntegrity   raw copy                   centroid   quantization
main          .vec .veq        .vec                       .vec       .vec          4
#16839        .vec .veq        .vec, centroid             -          .vec          3
this issue    -                .vec, centroid, checksum   -          .vec          2

"this issue" assumes #16839 is merged. .vex (HNSW only) keeps its full check in step 0.
``` 
Test proposal: flip one byte in each part of a source `.vec` and check if every merge fails. For merge performance, compare real force merges on Cohere 1M x 1024 between #16839 and this change , with a cold and a warm page cache , with random and block deletes, after that check both merge time and bytes read from disk.

Some ideas in foresee risks and mitigation plan:

- Error detection timing[@mikemccand mentioned]: `.vec` corruption is found during the raw copy instead of in step 0. ## Description

`BlockMaxConjunctionBulkScorer#score` loops while `windowMin < max`, but does not cap `max` at `maxDoc`. Whole-segment searches pass `NO_MORE_DOCS` as `max`.

If the final windows in a segment are non-competitive, they are skipped without advancing the lead scorer. As a result, scoring continues through approximately 32K empty 64K-document windows, up to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

This occurs with conjunctions of per-field disjunctions—for example, a MultiFieldQueryParser-style `a AND b` query:

```text
+(f1:a f2:a) +(f1:b f2:b)
```

under `TOP_SCORES`. In this case, `DisjunctionSumScorer#getMaxScore` excludes exhausted sub-scorers, leaving the score bound below the minimum competitive score.

On a 27.6M-document index, a two-term top-k query took 3.6 ms rather than 0.8 ms, with most of the additional time spent in `computeMaxScore`.

## Version and environment

Lucene 10.5.2 and main (`8476457`), using JDK 21 and 25.

## Fix and test

Fix and regression test: #16855.

While trying to find more unused classes within the current `main` branch, I also noticed `CachingExpressionValueSource` - but before deleting it a discussion might make sense.

Currently it's only referred to in a test - which would fail if replaced with `ExpressionValueSource`.

It seems this class was never wired in and implementation left a bit a incomplete, as it may need to overwrite `rewrite()` to work?

Also there was some discussion in apache/lucene#9620.

Happy to create a removal PR, if there is agreement.

body_text:
## Problem

When a dependency POM contributes a repository through a JDK/OS/`activeByDefault`-activated profile (the legitimate path, see #13100 / #13116 / #13141), that repository can declare a URL that shadows `central` or another well-known repository with a different (potentially malicious) URL.

Maven currently has no defense against this: the repository is accepted as-is and used for artifact resolution.

## Proposed Solution

Implement a WARN (or optionally FAIL with a flag) policy that triggers when:
- A repository contributed by an external-model profile has the same `<id>` as a repository already registered in the effective repository list (e.g. `central`), but a different URL.

This is a repository URL-mismatch check, scoped to the dependency resolution path.

## Non-goals

- This issue does **not** revert the fix in #13100 / #13116 / #13141. The blanket stripping was over-broad.
- The check should apply only when a conflict is detected, not as a general ban on external-model profile repositories.

## Notes

- Discussed in #13100 and deferred from #13141 (forward-port of #13116 to master).
- A `// TODO(#428)` marker has been added at the relevant call site in `DefaultModelBuilder` as a reminder.
- The redefinition concern is orthogonal to the activation fix and should be addressed as a separate hardening item.

body_text:
## Overview

This issue tracks the overall plan for addressing Maven's classloading architecture problems.

- **Classloading architecture reference** (current state + planned future): https://gist.github.com/gnodet/20f283d4a69c6df76b3164249f28b2e1
- **Original design document**: https://gist.github.com/gnodet/fef0571deb83280f1df60e7cce1307a1

## Use Cases

1. **Plugin/extension needs a core-provided package** — A plugin or extension needs a package available in Maven's core classloader imported into its own realm. Today they passively receive whatever core exports globally; they cannot request specific additional packages. *(MNG-7921, MNG-7955)*

2. **Shared types across plugins** — A library provides an SPI that multiple plugins implement or consume. Today, sharing types across plugin realms requires a fake `<extensions>true</extensions>` wrapper that exports globally. There is no way for a dependency to declare "these packages should be visible across realms" without being a plugin itself. *(Tycho SPI use case)*

3. **Plugin/extension needs JDK internal access** — A plugin or extension needs `--add-opens` or `--add-exports` for a JDK-internal package. Today the only option is a global JVM flag, which opens the package to all code rather than targeting a specific realm.

4. **Plugin/extension wants full JPMS module isolation** — A modern plugin or extension wants to run in its own `ModuleLayer` with proper module boundaries rather than flat classpath loading.

5. **Consistent behavior across all extension loading paths** — Extensions loaded via build `<extensions>`, core `.mvn/extensions.xml`, and `-Dmaven.ext.class.path` should all have the same capabilities (exports, imports, strategy). Today they diverge: ext classpath silently ignores descriptors, core extensions don't read artifact-level defaults.

6. **Deterministic conflict resolution** — When two extensions export the same package, behavior should be well-defined, not dependent on accidental ordering.

## Problem Statement

Maven's classloading architecture has several distinct but related problems:

1. **Global-only exports** — `META-INF/maven/extension.xml` `exportedPackages`/`exportedArtifacts` are injected into *all* plugin/extension realms via `CoreExports`. No per-consumer scoping.

2. **No import control for plugins/extensions** — plugins are passive recipients of whatever core globally exported. No way to say "I need package X in *my* realm only" (see #8997 / MNG-7921, MNG-7955).

3. **`maven.ext.class.path` gap** — entries on that system property bypass `extension.xml` discovery; their exports are silently ignored (see #10506 / MNG-8112, PR #13101 — currently targeting the wrong class).

4. **JPMS vs. unnamed module world** — PR #13490's `META-INF/maven/module-access` only helps named JPMS modules. The vast majority of plugins live in the unnamed module world and have no equivalent.

5. **Classworlds not owned** — `plexus-classworlds` is an external dependency Maven cannot evolve.

6. **Plugins have no descriptor-driven realm control** — `META-INF/maven/extension.xml` is read for extension-plugins (`<extensions>true</extensions>`) but **never read for regular plugins** at realm-creation time. `DefaultMavenPluginManager.createPluginRealm()` hardcodes the realm setup from `CoreExports` only; plugins cannot declare imports, exports, or a loading strategy. Extensions and plugins need the same fix but through different wiring paths.

7. **No way for plugins to declare required extensions** — A plugin that depends on a shared SPI library cannot declare "this dependency must be loaded as an extension." Today the SPI library must be wrapped in a fake `<extensions>true</extensions>` plugin, or users must explicitly add it as a `<build><extension>` in their POM.

## Solution Layers

### Layer 0 — Own the classloading stack (prerequisite)

Finish PR #13490: internalize `plexus-classworlds` as `impl/maven-classworlds`. All subsequent layers depend on Maven owning these types.

> **Note:** The original plan included a public API module (`api/maven-api-classworlds`). Per review feedback, the low-level `ClassWorld`/`ClassRealm` API module has been deferred — Layer 0 only internalizes the implementation. Instead, a higher-level public API is introduced (see Layer 0b below).

### Layer 0b — Public Realm API and Component Visibility

Introduce a single **`Realm`** interface that bundles a classloader, an optional JPMS module layer, and a scoped `Lookup`. The same interface is used at every level — session, project, plugin — with the difference being what the `Lookup` sees, not the type:

```java
/**
 * A runtime scope that bundles classloading with scoped component discovery.
 *
 * @since 4.1.0
 */
@Experimental
public interface Realm {

    /** The classloader for this realm. */
    @Nonnull
    ClassLoader classLoader();

    /** The JPMS module layer, if this realm runs in a modular configuration. */
    @Nonnull
    Optional<ModuleLayer> moduleLayer();

    /** Lookup scoped to this realm's visibility rules. */
    @Nonnull
    Lookup lookup();
}
```

Exposed uniformly:
- `Session.realm()` — core classloader, session-level `Lookup`, core module layer (if any, e.g. JLine per #13491)
- `Project.realm()` — project classloader (core + extension imports), project-scoped `Lookup`
- `Plugin.realm()` — plugin classloader, plugin-scoped `Lookup`, plugin module layer (if modular per Layer 4)

`Plugin.realm()` replaces `Plugin.getClassLoader()`. `session.realm().lookup()` subsumes `session.getService(Lookup.class)`.

#### Composed Lookups, not parent/child injectors

Visibility rules for components are **not a containment hierarchy**. Plugins do not inherit the project realm's classloader, and they do not inherit its components either. Each realm's `lookup()` is composed from explicit sources:

| Realm | `lookup()` sees |
|-------|----------------|
| `session.realm()` | Core + core extension components |
| `project.realm()` | Session components + exported components from this project's build extension realms |
| `plugin.realm()` | Explicitly seeded services (`InternalSession.getAllServices()`) + plugin classpath components + exported components from `requiredExtensions` (Layer 1) |

A parent/child injector model was considered and rejected: the project realm is a catch-all foreign import for plugin realms at the *class* level (`DefaultMavenPluginManager.calcImports()` maps `foreignImports.put("", projectRealm)`), but component visibility is intentionally narrower — plugins see only explicitly seeded services, not all core/project components. Component bridges from extensions into plugins require an explicit `requiredExtensions` declaration (Layer 1).

#### No `@ProjectScoped` annotation

The project realm's injector lifecycle **is** the scope boundary. Extension-contributed components are discovered when the extension realm's injector is created and are no longer reachable when it is disposed. No annotation is needed.

A `@ProjectScoped` scope annotation was considered and rejected: it would require per-thread binding (via `ThreadLocal` enter/exit) for concurrent reactor builds — effectively TCCL under a different name. Instead, project context is passed explicitly via the realm:

```java
// Explicit context — no thread-local, no TCCL
project.realm().lookup().lookup(PackagingRegistry.class).require(id);
```

#### Project realm structure

Each build extension has its own isolated `ClassRealm` and its own injector. The project realm **aggregates** these, mirroring how class imports work:
- **Class level:** `projectRealm.importFrom(extensionRealm, exportedPackage)` — selective class imports per extension, driven by `exportedPackages` in `extension.xml` (existing mechanism in `DefaultProjectBuildingHelper:186-250`)
- **Component level:** `project.realm().lookup()` composes a view over all extension realm injectors, filtered to each extension's exported components

#### Plugin realm keeps explicit seeding

`plugin.realm().lookup()` wraps the existing standalone plugin injector (created in `DefaultMavenPluginManager:569`). Plugins see only what is explicitly provided: session services, `Project`, `MojoExecution`, `Log`, and plugin classpath components. This is unchanged from the current model.

Layer 1's `requiredExtensions` adds a controlled bridge: exported components from declared required extensions become visible in the plugin's `lookup()`. Without the declaration, no extension components cross the boundary.

#### Component import/export in descriptors

Component visibility follows the same import/export model as class visibility, using the same `extension.xml` descriptor (format details in Layer 1):

- **Export side:** `exportedComponents` in `extension.xml`, parallel to `exportedPackages`. When `exportedComponents` is absent, all discoverable components in `exportedPackages` are exported by default (backward-compatible: existing extensions without an explicit `exportedComponents` element do not change behavior until they opt in).
- **Import side for plugins:** `requiredExtensions` in `plugin.xml` bridges both class imports and component imports from declared extensions.
- **Import side for projects:** declaring `<build><extensions>` is the import — `project.realm().lookup()` automatically aggregates exported components from all declared build extensions.

#### TCCL call sites replaced

The project realm is currently set as TCCL at ~9 call sites for Sisu's `FilteredBeans` component filtering. With `Realm`, these become explicit context passing:

| Call site | Current (TCCL) | New (explicit realm) |
|-----------|---------------|---------------------|
| `DefaultProject:59` | Set TCCL → `requirePackaging()` | `project.realm().lookup().lookup(PackagingRegistry.class)` |
| `DefaultMaven:466` | TCCL loop over projects → `lookupList()` | Iterate projects, use each `project.realm().lookup()` |
| `BuilderCommon:201` / `BuildPlanExecutor:1261` | `attachToThread(project)` | Pass realm to lifecycle execution |
| `LifecycleDependencyResolver:115` | Set TCCL before dependency resolution | Derive realm from `Project` |
| `DefaultProjectBuilder:519,1402` | `selectProjectRealm(project)` | Build `Realm` after extensions loaded |

#### Relationship to PR #13625

PR #13625 introduces a `PluginRealm` interface with `classLoader()`, `moduleLayer()`, `lookup()`. This should be renamed to `Realm` and generalized for session/project/plugin use. The `RealmLookup` implementation currently uses TCCL internally (swaps TCCL around each delegate call to leverage Sisu's `FilteredBeans`) — this is a correct transitional implementation. When realm-scoped injectors replace Sisu's filtering, only the `Lookup` implementation changes; the public `Realm` API is stable.

### Layer 1 — Per-realm import descriptor and required extensions

Extend `META-INF/maven/extension.xml` with import and strategy declarations so plugins/extensions can declare what they need imported into **their own realm only**:

```xml
<extension>
  <!-- EXISTING: what this artifact exports to ALL other realms -->
  <exportedPackages>...</exportedPackages>
  <exportedArtifacts>...</exportedArtifacts>

  <!-- NEW: what this plugin/extension needs imported into ITS OWN realm only -->
  <importedPackages>
    <importedPackage>org.slf4j</importedPackage>
    <importedPackage>com.google.inject</importedPackage>
  </importedPackages>
  <importedArtifacts>
    <importedArtifact>com.google.inject:guice</importedArtifact>
  </importedArtifacts>

  <!-- NEW: classloader loading strategy -->
  <classLoaderStrategy>self-first</classLoaderStrategy>

  <!-- NEW: component visibility (parallel to exportedPackages for classes) -->
  <exportedComponents>
    <exportedComponent>com.example.spi.AuthService</exportedComponent>
  </exportedComponents>
</extension>
```

Key design decisions:
- `importedPackages`/`importedArtifacts` restricted to packages already in `CoreExports` — plugins cannot reach core internals
- Descriptor read from primary artifact JAR only (not transitives) — avoids resolution chicken-and-egg
- `classLoaderStrategy` in `extension.xml` is the artifact-level default; `.mvn/extensions.xml` `<classLoadingStrategy>` remains the project-level override
- Applies to **both plugins and extensions**: `DefaultMavenPluginManager.createPluginRealm()` must read `extension.xml` from the plugin's primary JAR and honour the same fields. This is currently only done for extension-plugins.
- **Conflict resolution:** when two extensions export the same package, Maven must **fail with an error**. Extensions export their own classes (not third-party libraries), so duplicate exports indicate a genuine misconfiguration.
- **`exportedComponents`** declares which DI components are visible to consumers that import this extension (see Layer 0b). When absent, all discoverable components in `exportedPackages` are exported by default.

> **Note on naming:** `META-INF/maven/extension.xml` is an unfortunate historical name — it is already used by regular plugins (e.g. `maven-compiler-plugin` exports packages via it). The descriptor describes any Maven artifact's classloading contract, not just extensions. A future rename to `META-INF/maven/artifact.xml` or `META-INF/maven/classloading.xml` may be worth considering, with backward-compatible aliasing.

#### Required extensions in plugin descriptor

To solve the shared-types use case (use case 2) without adding a new mechanism, plugins can declare **required extensions** in their plugin descriptor (`META-INF/maven/plugin.xml`):

```xml
<plugin>
  ...
  <requiredExtensions>
    <requiredExtension>org.eclipse.tycho:tycho-spi</requiredExtension>
  </requiredExtensions>
</plugin>
```

When a plugin is loaded, Maven:
1. Reads `<requiredExtensions>` from the plugin descriptor
2. For each required extension, creates or reuses an extension realm (via the existing `ExtensionRealmCache`) from that dependency
3. Reads the dependency's own `META-INF/maven/extension.xml` for `exportedPackages` and `exportedComponents`
4. Imports those packages into the plugin's realm (class visibility) and those components into the plugin's `Lookup` (component visibility)
5. Excludes the dependency's JAR from the plugin's own classpath (to avoid class duplication)

This reuses the existing extension realm mechanism — no new concept. Extension realms are cached and shared: if multiple plugins declare the same `requiredExtension`, they share the same `ClassRealm` and see the same `Class` objects (type identity works for SPI `instanceof` checks).

The SPI library (`tycho-spi`) owns its own `extension.xml` declaring what it exports. The plugin (`tycho-maven-plugin`) just references it. No wrapper artifact needed, no `<build><extensions>` declaration needed in user POMs.

Solves #8997 (MNG-7921) and MNG-7955.

### Layer 2 — Non-JPMS module access control

Extend the same descriptor with module access for plugins and extensions in the unnamed module world:

```xml
<extension>
  ...
  <moduleAccess>
    <!-- targeted at this realm's classloader only, not ALL-UNNAMED -->
    <addOpens>java.base/sun.nio.ch</addOpens>
    <addExports>jdk.internal.misc/jdk.internal.misc</addExports>
  </moduleAccess>
</extension>
```

Subsumes and unifies PR #13490's `META-INF/maven/module-access` into a single descriptor.

Applies to both plugins and extensions: `DefaultMavenPluginManager` must call the module-access wiring after realm creation, not only `DefaultClassRealmManager` for extensions.

### Layer 3 — Fix `maven.ext.class.path` (replaces PR #13101)

In `PlexusContainerCapsuleFactory` (`o.a.maven.cling.invoker`, `impl/maven-cli` — **not** `MavenCli` in deprecated `compat/maven-embedder`): discover `extension.xml` from `maven.ext.class.path` entries, deduplicate by canonical path, include exports in `CoreExports`.

### Layer 4 — Per-plugin/extension JPMS ModuleLayer

A plugin or extension can opt into full JPMS module isolation via `<modular>true</modular>` in its descriptor. Maven creates an isolated per-plugin/extension `ModuleLayer` via `Configuration.resolveAndBind()` + `defineModulesWithOneLoader()`. Dependencies are resolved as JPMS modules with proper `requires`/`exports` boundaries.

Key design points:
- `ClassRealm` gains `getModuleLayer()`, `isModular()`, `addExports()`, `addOpens()` for module access control
- `PluginRealmCache` keys encode the `modular` flag
- No fallback — a modular plugin/extension that cannot be loaded as a module causes a hard error
- Applies to both plugins and extensions

## Design Principle — Component Visibility Follows Classloading Rules

Today, DI component visibility is an implicit side-effect of Sisu's realm-based `FilteredBeans` mechanism. Components in non-imported realms are silently hidden at lookup time. This is extremely hard to debug: a missing component produces no error — it simply doesn't appear in injected collections or lookups, with no indication that realm visibility is the cause.

**Going forward, component visibility must be explicit and follow the realm import chain:**

A component is visible to a consumer if and only if the component's realm is in the consumer's import chain. This is the same import chain that `extension.xml` defines for classes — one set of rules for both class loading and component discovery.

**Scoping rules:**

| Component source | Visible to |
|---|---|
| Core / core extensions | All projects and plugins (in `CoreExports`) |
| Build extensions | Only projects that declare the extension (imported into project realm) |
| Required extensions | Only plugins that declare them (imported into plugin realm) |
| Plugins | Only within the plugin's own execution (isolated realm) |

This scoping is critical: a custom packaging registered by a build extension in Project A must NOT be visible in Project B if Project B doesn't declare that extension. Today Sisu achieves this via `FilteredBeans` + TCCL (Thread Context ClassLoader) — when Maven processes Project A, lookups are filtered through Project A's realm imports; Project B sees a different set.

**What needs to change:** `maven-di` (`InjectorImpl`) currently has no realm-based visibility — all bindings are flat within each injector instance. The target model uses **per-realm injectors** whose `Lookup` views are composed from explicit import/export rules:

- Each extension realm gets its own injector, discovering components from its classloader
- `project.realm().lookup()` aggregates exported components from the project's extension realm injectors
- `plugin.realm().lookup()` exposes explicit seeds + plugin classpath + `requiredExtensions` exports
- Component import/export rules are declared in `extension.xml` (`exportedComponents`) and `plugin.xml` (`requiredExtensions`), mirroring class-level `exportedPackages`
- Project context is passed explicitly via `project.realm()` — no TCCL, no thread-local scope

During the Sisu transition, realm `Lookup` implementations can delegate to Sisu's `FilteredBeans` via TCCL (as PR #13625 does). When Sisu is removed, the per-realm injectors handle visibility natively. The public `Realm` API is stable across this transition.

**Error reporting:** when a component is not found due to realm visibility, the DI container must produce a clear error naming the missing import and the realm boundary — not a silent empty result.

## Component Map

| Component | Change |
|---|---|
| `impl/maven-classworlds` | New module: inlined classworlds implementation (Layer 0 / #13490) |
| `api/maven-api-core` `Realm` | New interface: classloader + optional `ModuleLayer` + scoped `Lookup` (Layer 0b); replaces `PluginRealm` from #13625 |
| `api/maven-api-core` `Session` | Add `realm()` returning session-level `Realm` (Layer 0b) |
| `api/maven-api-core` `Project` | Add `realm()` returning project-level `Realm` (Layer 0b) |
| `api/maven-api-core` `Plugin` | `realm()` replaces `getClassLoader()` (Layer 0b / #13625) |
| `impl/maven-core` `DefaultPluginManager` | Build `Realm` with composed `Lookup`; **process `<requiredExtensions>` from `plugin.xml`**: bridge exported components from declared extensions into plugin `Lookup` (Layer 0b + Layer 1) |
| `impl/maven-core` `DefaultProjectBuildingHelper` | Build `Realm` with composed `Lookup` aggregating exported components from extension realms (Layer 0b); also apply `importedPackages` on the class side (Layer 1) |
| `impl/maven-core` `ExtensionDescriptor` | Add: importedPackages, importedArtifacts, classLoaderStrategy, **exportedComponents**, moduleAddOpens, moduleAddExports |
| `impl/maven-core` `ExtensionDescriptorBuilder` | Add: parsing of the new elements |
| `impl/maven-core` `DefaultClassRealmManager` | Apply per-realm descriptor: targeted imports, module access, strategy (extensions + extension-plugins) |
| `impl/maven-core` `DefaultMavenPluginManager` | **Read `extension.xml` from plugin primary JAR at realm-creation time** (currently only done for extension-plugins); apply importedPackages, classLoaderStrategy, moduleAccess for regular plugins; **process `<requiredExtensions>` from `plugin.xml`**: create/reuse extension realms for declared dependencies |
| `impl/maven-core` `PluginRealmCache.Key` | Must capture descriptor-driven fields (importedPackages, classLoaderStrategy, modular) — otherwise two projects referencing the same plugin coordinates but with different realm descriptors would share a stale cached realm |
| `impl/maven-core` plugin descriptor model | Add `<requiredExtensions>` element to `plugin.xml` schema |
| `impl/maven-cli` `BootstrapCoreExtensionManager` | Core extensions realm-creation path: already applies project-level `<classLoadingStrategy>` from `CoreExtension` model but never reads the artifact-level `extension.xml` descriptor; needs Layer 1 wiring |
| `impl/maven-cli` `PlexusContainerCapsuleFactory` | Fix maven.ext.class.path discovery with path dedup |
| `compat/maven-embedder` | **No new logic** — deprecated |

## Realm Creation Paths

All realm-creation paths must converge on the same descriptor handling after these changes:

| Path | Component | Reads `extension.xml` today? | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regular plugins | `DefaultMavenPluginManager.createPluginRealm()` | **No** | Layer 1: read descriptor, apply imports/strategy; process `requiredExtensions` |
| Extension-plugins (`<extensions>true</extensions>`) | `DefaultMavenPluginManager` | Yes (exports only) | Layer 1: also apply imports/strategy |
| Build extensions (`<build><extensions>`) | `DefaultProjectBuildingHelper` → `DefaultClassRealmManager.createExtensionRealm()` | Yes (exports only) | Layer 1: also apply imports/strategy |
| Core extensions (`.mvn/extensions.xml`) | `BootstrapCoreExtensionManager` | **No** (project-level strategy only) | Layer 1: read artifact-level descriptor as fallback |
| `maven.ext.class.path` | `PlexusContainerCapsuleFactory` | **No** | Layer 3: discover and apply descriptors |

## Sequencing

1. **Layer 0** — finish #13490 (classworlds internalization)
2. **Layer 0b** — public Realm API (#13625 reworked)
3. **Layer 3** — rework #13101 targeting `impl/maven-cli` only
4. **Layer 1** — descriptor import/strategy extension + `requiredExtensions` + `exportedComponents`, core of the feature
5. **Layer 2** — module access, follows Layer 1, same descriptor format
6. **Layer 4** — per-plugin/extension JPMS ModuleLayer (#13494)

> **Layer 3 / Layer 1 coupling:** Layer 1 restricts `importedPackages` to packages already in `CoreExports`. If a `maven.ext.class.path` extension exports a package (Layer 3), that package should be importable via `importedPackages` (Layer 1). Delivering Layer 3 before Layer 1 is therefore correct — but if Layer 3 ships first, any daemon-mode build must not reuse `PluginRealmCache` entries built before Layer 3 exports landed (i.e. before `PlexusContainerCapsuleFactory` registered those exports into `CoreExports`).
