### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).
- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I have confirmed that this bug belongs to the current repository, not other repositories of RocketMQ.

### Runtime platform environment

OS: any (client side, `DefaultMQPushConsumer`)

### RocketMQ version

branch: develop
Git commit id: a7edeecfb

### JDK Version

Compiler: Temurin 1.8.0_504 (target 1.8, same as CI)

### Describe the Bug

`DefaultMQPushConsumerImpl.start()` creates **and starts** two consume services, but `shutdown()` stops only the first one:

```java
this.consumeMessageService.start();
// POPTODO
this.consumeMessagePopService.start();       // DefaultMQPushConsumerImpl.java:984-986
```

```java
case RUNNING:
    this.consumeMessageService.shutdown(awaitTerminateMillis);      // :908 — the pop service is never stopped
```

The pop service is not idle after it is started: `ConsumeMessagePopOrderlyService.start()` schedules `lockMQPeriodically()` at a fixed rate on a single-thread executor created with `new ThreadFactoryImpl("ConsumeMessageScheduledThread_")` (`client/.../ConsumeMessagePopOrderlyService.java:64-77`), and `ThreadFactoryImpl` creates **non-daemon** threads by default (`common/.../ThreadFactoryImpl.java:35`, `:59`). `ConsumeMessagePopConcurrentlyService.start()` likewise starts its consume executor. Both services implement `shutdown(long)` (`ConsumeMessagePopOrderlyService.java:80-88`, `ConsumeMessagePopConcurrentlyService.java:70`), and no code in the client module ever calls it — the only references to the field are the two assignments, `start()` and `submitPopConsumeRequest`.

The same omission exists in the failed-start branch, which stops only `consumeMessageService` when the consumer group is already registered (`DefaultMQPushConsumerImpl.java:991-993`).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `DefaultMQPushConsumer consumer = new DefaultMQPushConsumer("group"); consumer.subscribe("topic", "*"); consumer.registerMessageListener(listener);`
2. `consumer.start(); consumer.shutdown();`
3. The pop service is still running: for CLUSTERING (the default) the `ConsumeMessageScheduledThread_` thread keeps firing `lockMQPeriodically()` every `REBALANCE_LOCK_INTERVAL` on an empty process-queue table, the threads are non-daemon, so a JVM that relies on the consumer's shutdown to release its resources never terminates.

At the unit level the existing harness covers it: `DefaultMQPushConsumerImplTest` already injects a mocked `consumeMessagePopService` (line ~250-254) and has a `testShutdown`, so asserting that the service is shut down with `shutdown()` fails deterministically today.

### What Did You Expect to See?

`DefaultMQPushConsumer.shutdown()` "shut down this client and releasing underlying resources" (`client/.../consumer/DefaultMQPushConsumer.java:789`) — i.e. both consume services are stopped, exactly like the non-pop one in the same method. The pop services' own `shutdown(long)` methods are the proof that this was the intent.

### What Did You See Instead?

After `shutdown()` the consumer's pop scheduler (and, for pop consumers, the pop consume executor) keeps running with non-daemon threads; the client appears stopped (`serviceState = SHUTDOWN_ALREADY`) while resources are still held, which can leave the JVM unable to exit.

### Additional Context

Minimal fix: stop `consumeMessagePopService` next to `consumeMessageService` in both places — the normal shutdown path and the register-failure path.

I will open a PR with those two one-line changes plus a regression test in `DefaultMQPushConsumerImplTest` (red before: the pop service receives no `shutdown` call).

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).
- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I have confirmed that this bug belongs to the current repository, not other repositories of RocketMQ.

### Runtime platform environment

OS: any (broker with the RocksDB config manager: `enableRocksDBStore=true`, i.e. `RocksDBSubscriptionGroupManager`)

### RocketMQ version

branch: develop
Git commit id: a7edeecfb

### JDK Version

Compiler: Temurin 1.8.0_504 (target 1.8, same as CI)

### Describe the Bug

The RocksDB variant of the subscription group manager persists the group's forbidden bits with `JSON.toJSONString(this.getForbiddenTable().get(group))`, and after the last bit of a group is cleared the table no longer holds an entry for that group — so the value written to the `forbidden` column family is the **string `"null"`**:

```java
@Override
public void updateForbidden(String group, String topic, int forbiddenIndex, boolean setOrClear) {
    super.updateForbidden(group, topic, forbiddenIndex, setOrClear);
    this.rocksDBConfigManager.put(FORBIDDEN_COLUMN_FAMILY_NAME, group,
        JSON.toJSONString(this.getForbiddenTable().get(group)));   // -> "null" once the group has no forbidden bits left
}
```

The same shape appears in `setForbidden` and `clearForbidden` (`broker/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/broker/config/v1/RocksDBSubscriptionGroupManager.java:287-306`; the `updateForbidden` variant is at `:276-284`).

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).
- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.

### Runtime platform environment

OS: any (the `mqadmin` tool)

### RocketMQ version

branch: develop
Git commit id: a7edeecfb

### JDK Version

Compiler: Temurin 1.8.0_504 (target 1.8, same as CI)

### Describe the Bug

`tools/src/main/resources/rmq.tools.logback.xml` — the configuration the distribution installs as `conf/rmq.tools.logback.xml` and that `mqadmin` selects with `-Drmq.logback.configurationFile` (`distribution/bin/mqadmin:45`) — attaches three loggers to an appender it never defines:

```xml
<logger name="RocketmqCommon" additivity="false" level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="RocketmqBrokerAppender"/>     <!-- not defined in this file -->
</logger>
<logger name="RocketmqStore" additivity="false" level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="RocketmqBrokerAppender"/>
</logger>
<logger name="RocketmqRemoting" additivity="false" level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="RocketmqBrokerAppender"/>
</logger>
```

The appenders this file defines are `DefaultAppender`, `RocketmqToolsAppender`, `RocketmqToolsAppender_inner` and `STDOUT`; `RocketmqBrokerAppender` only exists in the *broker* and *proxy* configurations, and logback resolves `appender-ref`s inside the configuration file that is being loaded, so the reference cannot be satisfied.

The consequence is user-visible and completely silent: those loggers also set `additivity="false"`, so once their only `appender-ref` is dropped they are attached to **no appender at all** — everything logged through `RocketmqCommon`, `RocketmqStore` and `RocketmqRemoting` is discarded and nothing from the client/store/remoting layers reaches `tools.log` (or any other appender), which is exactly the diagnostic trail an operator needs when a tool misbehaves. I verified with the project's own loader (`JoranConfiguratorExt`, the class the runtime uses) and a status collector that this logback build reports **no status message at all** for the unresolved reference — no warning, no error, so the loss is not even visible in the tool's output.

The sibling configurations do this correctly, which is the pattern to keep: broker points those loggers at its own `RocketmqBrokerAppender`, namesrv at `RocketmqNamesrvAppender` (`namesrv/src/main/resources/rmq.namesrv.logback.xml:94-100`), proxy at its `RocketmqBrokerAppender`. This is the same class of mistake that was fixed in #11177 (an appender registered under a name that did not match its definition).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run any admin command, e.g. `mqadmin clusterList -n 127.0.0.1:9876` (the wrapper passes `conf/rmq.tools.logback.xml`).
2. Check `${user.home}/logs/rocketmqlogs/tools.log`: nothing logged by `RocketmqCommon`/`RocketmqStore`/`RocketmqRemoting` ever appears there, and no message is printed about the dropped configuration either.

At the unit level the shipped file is loaded with the project's own `JoranConfiguratorExt` (`common/.../logging/JoranConfiguratorExt.java`, the loader that also rewrites the unshaded logback class names for the shaded runtime) into a fresh logger context: the three loggers end up with no appender, and the loader reports no error or warning for it.

### What Did You Expect to See?

`mqadmin` starts without configuration errors, and its component loggers write to the tool's own log file — i.e. the three loggers reference `RocketmqToolsAppender` (the appender the file defines and that `RocketmqTools` already uses, writing to `${user.home}/logs/rocketmqlogs/tools.log`), mirroring how each other component points those loggers at its own appender.

### What Did You See Instead?

Three logback errors on every invocation and three loggers whose output is silently discarded.

### Additional Context

Minimal fix: replace the three `RocketmqBrokerAppender` references with `RocketmqToolsAppender`. I checked the other shipped configurations for the same mistake: only this file references an appender it does not define (the controller file defines `RocketmqControllerConsole` twice, but with identical content, which logback merges harmlessly).

I will open a PR with the three-line change plus a regression test that loads the shipped `rmq.tools.logback.xml` through `JoranConfiguratorExt` and asserts the three loggers are attached to an appender (red before: `RocketmqCommon must be attached to an appender`).

Compiler: Temurin 1.8.0_504 (target 1.8, same as CI)

### Describe the Bug

`tools/src/main/resources/rmq.tools.logback.xml` — the configuration the distribution installs as `conf/rmq.tools.logback.xml` and that `mqadmin` selects with `-Drmq.logback.configurationFile` (`distribution/bin/mqadmin:45`) — attaches three loggers to an appender it never defines:

```xml
<logger name="RocketmqCommon" additivity="false" level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="RocketmqBrokerAppender"/>     <!-- not defined in this file -->
</logger>
<logger name="RocketmqStore" additivity="false" level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="RocketmqBrokerAppender"/>
</logger>
<logger name="RocketmqRemoting" additivity="false" level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="RocketmqBrokerAppender"/>
</logger>
```

The appenders this file defines are `DefaultAppender`, `RocketmqToolsAppender`, `RocketmqToolsAppender_inner` and `STDOUT`; `RocketmqBrokerAppender` only exists in the *broker* and *proxy* configurations, and logback resolves `appender-ref`s inside the configuration file that is being loaded, so the reference cannot be satisfied.

The consequence is user-visible and completely silent: those loggers also set `additivity="false"`, so once their only `appender-ref` is dropped they are attached to **no appender at all** — everything logged through `RocketmqCommon`, `RocketmqStore` and `RocketmqRemoting` is discarded and nothing from the client/store/remoting layers reaches `tools.log` (or any other appender), which is exactly the diagnostic trail an operator needs when a tool misbehaves. I verified with the project's own loader (`JoranConfiguratorExt`, the class the runtime uses) and a status collector that this logback build reports **no status message at all** for the unresolved reference — no warning, no error, so the loss is not even visible in the tool's output.

The sibling configurations do this correctly, which is the pattern to keep: broker points those loggers at its own `RocketmqBrokerAppender`, namesrv at `RocketmqNamesrvAppender` (`namesrv/src/main/resources/rmq.namesrv.logback.xml:94-100`), proxy at its `RocketmqBrokerAppender`. This is the same class of mistake that was fixed in #11177 (an appender registered under a name that did not match its definition).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run any admin command, e.g. `mqadmin clusterList -n 127.0.0.1:9876` (the wrapper passes `conf/rmq.tools.logback.xml`).
2. Check `${user.home}/logs/rocketmqlogs/tools.log`: nothing logged by `RocketmqCommon`/`RocketmqStore`/`RocketmqRemoting` ever appears there, and no message is printed about the dropped configuration either.

At the unit level the shipped file is loaded with the project's own `JoranConfiguratorExt` (`common/.../logging/JoranConfiguratorExt.java`, the loader that also rewrites the unshaded logback class names for the shaded runtime) into a fresh logger context: the three loggers end up with no appender, and the loader reports no error or warning for it.

### What Did You Expect to See?

`mqadmin` starts without configuration errors, and its component loggers write to the tool's own log file — i.e. the three loggers reference `RocketmqToolsAppender` (the appender the file defines and that `RocketmqTools` already uses, writing to `${user.home}/logs/rocketmqlogs/tools.log`), mirroring how each other component points those loggers at its own appender.

### What Did You See Instead?

Three logback errors on every invocation and three loggers whose output is silently discarded.

### Additional Context

Minimal fix: replace the three `RocketmqBrokerAppender` references with `RocketmqToolsAppender`. I checked the other shipped configurations for the same mistake: only this file references an appender it does not define (the controller file defines `RocketmqControllerConsole` twice, but with identical content, which logback merges harmlessly).

I will open a PR with the three-line change plus a regression test that loads the shipped `rmq.tools.logback.xml` through `JoranConfiguratorExt` and asserts the three loggers are attached to an appender (red before: `RocketmqCommon must be attached to an appender`).

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).

- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.

- [x] I have confirmed that this bug belongs to the current repository, not other repositories of RocketMQ.

### Runtime platform environment

Any.

### RocketMQ version

develop branch (dc70260b7)

### JDK Version

Any.

### Describe the Bug

`PopLiteLongPollingService` keeps suspended lite long-polling requests in per-client queues stored in `pollingMap`. Both wake-up paths — `notifyMessageArriving()` and the timeout sweep in `run()` — reach a request **only through `pollingMap`**:

```java
// notifyMessageArriving()
ConcurrentSkipListSet<PopRequest> remotingCommands = pollingMap.get(pollingKey);
if (remotingCommands == null || remotingCommands.isEmpty()) {
    return false;
}
```

```java
// run() timeout sweep
for (Map.Entry<String, ConcurrentSkipListSet<PopRequest>> entry : pollingMap.entrySet()) { ... }
```

There are two ways a queue holding a **live, suspended** request disappears from `pollingMap` while `polling()` is adding to it:

**1. Race with `cleanUnusedResource()` (introduced by #10072).** Since #10072, the periodic cleanup removes entries whose queue is *empty*:

```java
pollingMap.entrySet().removeIf(entry -> CollectionUtils.isEmpty(entry.getValue()));
```

`polling()` (called on processor threads) first reads the queue and only later adds to it:

```java
ConcurrentSkipListSet<PopRequest> queue = pollingMap.get(pollingKey);   // (1) read
if (queue == null) { ... } else {
    int size = queue.size();                                            // (2) size check
    if (size > ...getPopPollingSize()) { return POLLING_FULL; }
}
if (queue.add(request)) {                                               // (3) add
    remotingCommand.setSuspended(true);
    ...
    return POLLING_SUC;                                                 // (4) client told "suspended OK"
}
```

The queue is routinely empty at (1): the last pending request was just woken by the timeout sweep or by `notifyMessageArriving()`, leaving the empty queue in the map. If the service thread's `cleanUnusedResource()` runs between (1)/(2) and (3), the entry is removed from `pollingMap`, and (3) adds the request to the now-orphaned queue. `polling()` still returns `POLLING_SUC`, so the caller treats the request as suspended — but neither `notifyMessageArriving()` nor the timeout sweep can ever find it. The classic `PopLongPollingService` does not have this race because its cleanup only removes queues whose topic/group metadata is gone, never on emptiness.

**2. Capacity eviction.** `pollingMap` is a `ConcurrentLinkedHashMap` with `maximumWeightedCapacity(popPollingMapSize)` (default 100000). Neither POLLING_FULL check (`maxPopPollingSize`, `popPollingSize`) bounds the number of *distinct keys*, so once the map is at capacity, inserting a new client's queue silently evicts an LRU entry — even when its queue still holds suspended requests — with the same unreachable-request consequence.

Impact: a suspended lite pop request is never answered by the broker — no message notification and no broker-side `POLLING_TIMEOUT`. The client blocks until its own (typically much longer) remoting invoke timeout, then sees a timeout error and re-polls. No message is lost (offsets are unaffected); this is a latency/availability defect of the lite polling path.

### Steps to Reproduce

Deterministic unit-level reproduction in `PopLiteLongPollingServiceTest` (JUnit 4 + Mockito, same harness as the existing tests):

1. Seed the routine post-sweep state: an **empty** queue for `clientId` in `pollingMap` (reflection field access, as the existing tests already do).
2. Gate the interleaving: override `BrokerConfig#getPopPollingSize()` (called by `polling()` between the `get()` and the `add()`) to block on a latch.
3. Start a thread calling `polling(ctx, cmd, now, 10000, clientId, group)`; wait until it parks inside the size check.
4. On the test thread, invoke `cleanUnusedResource()` via reflection — the empty entry is removed from `pollingMap`.
5. Release the latch; `polling()` completes and returns `POLLING_SUC`.
6. Assert the invariant: the suspended request must stay reachable through `pollingMap` (`assertSame(queue, pollingMap.get(clientId))`, then `notifyMessageArriving()` must return `true`).

For the eviction path: build the service with `popPollingMapSize = 1`, poll for `clientA` (POLLING_SUC), then poll for `clientB` — `clientA`'s queue is evicted while holding its suspended request, and no wake-up is ever submitted for it.

### What Did You Expect to See?

Every request for which `polling()` returns `POLLING_SUC` stays reachable through `pollingMap`, so it is woken by `notifyMessageArriving()` on message arrival or answered with `POLLING_TIMEOUT` by the sweep in `run()` when its poll time elapses.

### What Did You See Instead?

`polling()` returns `POLLING_SUC` while the request lives in a queue that is no longer referenced by `pollingMap`:

- `notifyMessageArriving(clientId, ...)` returns `false` (map lookup misses),
- the timeout sweep in `run()` never sees the queue,

so the request hangs until the client-side remoting timeout fires.

### Additional Context

The empty-queue removal was introduced by #10072 (which fixed a different bug: cleaning up polling structures of unsubscribed clients without returning results). The race is a narrow-window regression of that simplification; the eviction path additionally requires more than `popPollingMapSize` distinct polling clientIds. The proposed fix keeps #10072's cleanup semantics: re-establish the mapping after a successful `add()` in `polling()` (failing the polling attempt fast if another poller has meanwhile re-created the queue), and wake up the requests of a queue that is evicted at capacity.

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).

- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.

- [x] I have confirmed that this bug belongs to the current repository, not other repositories of RocketMQ.

### Runtime platform environment

Any.

### RocketMQ version

develop branch (dc70260b7)

### JDK Version

Any.

### Describe the Bug

`PopLiteMessageProcessor#preCheck` reserves a log slot for the consumer when the parent topic of a lite pop request does not exist, but never passes the argument:

```java
TopicConfig topicConfig = brokerController.getTopicConfigManager().selectTopicConfig(requestHeader.getTopic());
if (null == topicConfig) {
    LOGGER.error("The parentTopic {} not exist, consumer: {} ", requestHeader.getTopic());
    response.setCode(ResponseCode.TOPIC_NOT_EXIST);
    ...
}
```

The message template has two `{}` placeholders but only one argument. With SLF4J semantics the second placeholder is rendered literally, so the log line is:

```
The parentTopic xxx not exist, consumer: {}
```

The consumer group (available in `PopLiteMessageRequestHeader#getConsumerGroup()`) never appears. When a parent topic is deleted or a client is misconfigured, this ERROR is the only server-side trace of affected consumers — without the group, operators cannot tell who is impacted.

### Steps to Reproduce

Unit-level, deterministic (`PopLiteMessageProcessorTest` harness):

1. Build a `PopLiteMessageRequestHeader` with a topic that `TopicConfigManager#selectTopicConfig` returns `null` for and `consumerGroup = "groupA"`.
2. Call `popLiteMessageProcessor.preCheck(ctx, requestHeader, response)`; it returns `TOPIC_NOT_EXIST`.
3. Capture the formatted log event for logger `RocketmqPopLite`: the message is `The parentTopic xxx not exist, consumer: {}` — `groupA` is absent.

### What Did You Expect to See?

`The parentTopic xxx not exist, consumer: groupA`

### What Did You See Instead?

`The parentTopic xxx not exist, consumer: {}`

### Additional Context

Only this line in the lite pop path has a placeholder/argument mismatch (verified by scanning all `LOGGER`/`POP_LOGGER` calls in `PopLiteMessageProcessor`, `LiteEventDispatcher`, `LiteSubscriptionRegistryImpl`, `PopLiteLongPollingService` and `NotificationProcessor` for the lite area). The sibling processor `NotificationProcessor` logs the remote address in the equivalent branch, so the pattern of identifying the caller is established — here the consumer group from the request header is the natural identifier.

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).
- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I have confirmed that this bug belongs to the current repository, not other repositories of RocketMQ.

### Runtime platform environment

OS: any (client-side SQL92 filter parsing: `MessageSelector.bySql(...)` / `FilterAPI`, and the broker-side compile of the same expression)

### RocketMQ version

branch: develop
Git commit id: 0dd48c39d

### JDK Version

Compiler: Temurin 1.8.0_504 (target 1.8, same as CI)

### Describe the Bug

The generated SQL92 parser never checks that the whole selector was consumed — its start rule parses one expression and returns:

```java
final public BooleanExpression JmsSelector() throws ParseException {
    Expression left = orExpression();
    return asBooleanExpression(left);
}
```

(`filter/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/parser/SelectorParser.java:99-102`; there is no `jj_consume_token(0)` anywhere in the file, and the grammar source has the same rule without `<EOF>` — `filter/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/parser/SelectorParser.jj:200-211`.)

So anything after a syntactically complete expression is silently thrown away, and the truncated expression is returned as if it were the whole filter:

- `SelectorParser.parse("a = 3 b = 4")` returns `(a = 3)` — the second clause is dropped instead of being reported as a syntax error (a user who forgets `AND` gets exactly this);
- `SelectorParser.parse("a < 10bbbbb")` returns `(a < 10)`.

Verified today on this tree: `filter/src/test/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/ParserTest.java` with two assertions that expect `MQFilterException` for these inputs fails with `Expecting value to be false but was true`, i.e. both parses succeed.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Client side: `consumer.subscribe(topic, MessageSelector.bySql("a = 3 b = 4"))` (or `FilterAPI.build(topic, "a = 3 b = 4", SQL92)`): no exception is raised, the subscription is registered with the expression `a = 3`.
2. Broker side: `ConsumerFilterManager.build` compiles the same expression, `FilterFactory.INSTANCE.get(SQL92).compile(...)` → `SqlFilter.compile` → `SelectorParser.parse` (`filter/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/SqlFilter.java:36`) succeeds, so the filter data is built for the truncated expression.
3. Consumers in the group then receive messages that violate the dropped clause (e.g. `b != 4`), with no error anywhere — the only signal a user could notice is the filter behaving as if half of it did not exist.

### What Did You Expect to See?

A selector that does not match the grammar is rejected with `MQFilterException` ("Invalid MessageSelector."), the way every other malformed selector is — this is the behaviour the module's own test intent encodes (`ParserTest.testParse_invalid` asserts that an input the grammar cannot accept raises `MQFilterException`), and the behaviour of the grammar this file is ported from, whose start rule is `orExpression() <EOF>`.

### What Did You See Instead?

The parse succeeds with a prefix of the selector, so a malformed filter is accepted and silently applied in its truncated form — messages that the user's filter excludes are delivered instead of the subscription failing fast.

### Additional Context

Prior art, for full context: PR #602 (2018) added the end-of-input token to the grammar for exactly these cases and was closed with "close due to time too long and wrong to merge to master, welcome to create a new PR to the apache: develop branch" — this report is that change against the current `develop`, where the defect still reproduces.

Minimal fix: consume the end-of-input token at the end of the start rule (`jj_consume_token(0)` in the generated parser, `<EOF>` in the grammar source so both stay in sync). Valid selectors are unaffected; any selector with trailing tokens now fails at parse time with the same `MQFilterException` as other invalid selectors. Note that `filter/pom.xml` has no JavaCC plugin, so the generated parser is the checked-in source of truth and the grammar file is updated for consistency only.

I will open a PR with the fix plus regression tests in `ParserTest` (red before: both parses return an expression; green after: both raise `MQFilterException`).

Compiler: Temurin 1.8.0_504 (target 1.8, same as CI)

### Describe the Bug

The generated SQL92 parser never checks that the whole selector was consumed — its start rule parses one expression and returns:

```java
final public BooleanExpression JmsSelector() throws ParseException {
    Expression left = orExpression();
    return asBooleanExpression(left);
}
```

(`filter/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/parser/SelectorParser.java:99-102`; there is no `jj_consume_token(0)` anywhere in the file, and the grammar source has the same rule without `<EOF>` — `filter/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/parser/SelectorParser.jj:200-211`.)

So anything after a syntactically complete expression is silently thrown away, and the truncated expression is returned as if it were the whole filter:

- `SelectorParser.parse("a = 3 b = 4")` returns `(a = 3)` — the second clause is dropped instead of being reported as a syntax error (a user who forgets `AND` gets exactly this);
- `SelectorParser.parse("a < 10bbbbb")` returns `(a < 10)`.

Verified today on this tree: `filter/src/test/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/ParserTest.java` with two assertions that expect `MQFilterException` for these inputs fails with `Expecting value to be false but was true`, i.e. both parses succeed.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Client side: `consumer.subscribe(topic, MessageSelector.bySql("a = 3 b = 4"))` (or `FilterAPI.build(topic, "a = 3 b = 4", SQL92)`): no exception is raised, the subscription is registered with the expression `a = 3`.
2. Broker side: `ConsumerFilterManager.build` compiles the same expression, `FilterFactory.INSTANCE.get(SQL92).compile(...)` → `SqlFilter.compile` → `SelectorParser.parse` (`filter/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/filter/SqlFilter.java:36`) succeeds, so the filter data is built for the truncated expression.
3. Consumers in the group then receive messages that violate the dropped clause (e.g. `b != 4`), with no error anywhere — the only signal a user could notice is the filter behaving as if half of it did not exist.

### What Did You Expect to See?

A selector that does not match the grammar is rejected with `MQFilterException` ("Invalid MessageSelector."), the way every other malformed selector is — this is the behaviour the module's own test intent encodes (`ParserTest.testParse_invalid` asserts that an input the grammar cannot accept raises `MQFilterException`), and the behaviour of the grammar this file is ported from, whose start rule is `orExpression() <EOF>`.

### What Did You See Instead?

The parse succeeds with a prefix of the selector, so a malformed filter is accepted and silently applied in its truncated form — messages that the user's filter excludes are delivered instead of the subscription failing fast.

### Additional Context

Prior art, for full context: PR #602 (2018) added the end-of-input token to the grammar for exactly these cases and was closed with "close due to time too long and wrong to merge to master, welcome to create a new PR to the apache: develop branch" — this report is that change against the current `develop`, where the defect still reproduces.

Minimal fix: consume the end-of-input token at the end of the start rule (`jj_consume_token(0)` in the generated parser, `<EOF>` in the grammar source so both stay in sync). Valid selectors are unaffected; any selector with trailing tokens now fails at parse time with the same `MQFilterException` as other invalid selectors. Note that `filter/pom.xml` has no JavaCC plugin, so the generated parser is the checked-in source of truth and the grammar file is updated for consistency only.

I will open a PR with the fix plus regression tests in `ParserTest` (red before: both parses return an expression; green after: both raise `MQFilterException`).

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).
- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I have confirmed that this bug belongs to the current repository, not other repositories of RocketMQ.

### Runtime platform environment

OS: any (broker hosting a compaction topic; the compaction round runs on a schedule, default `compactionScheduleInternal` = 15 min)

### RocketMQ version

branch: develop
Git commit id: 0dd48c39d

### JDK Version

Compiler: Temurin 1.8.0_504 (target 1.8, same as CI)

### Describe the Bug

Each compaction round writes its output into a *scratch* sub-folder and only moves it into the live compaction log when the round completes:

- `CompactionLog.compaction(...)` creates the scratch log with `compacting = new TopicPartitionLog(this, COMPACTING_SUB_FOLDER)` (`store/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/store/kv/CompactionLog.java:682`); the constructor only wires the paths (`:992-1006`) — it neither loads nor cleans the folder;
- the scratch folder is cleaned **only on the success path**: `replaceFiles(...)` (`:618`) moves the files out and `compacting.clean(false, false)` (`:621`) then verifies the folder is empty and throws otherwise (`TopicPartitionLog.clean(MappedFileQueue)`, `:1095-1104`). That check walks the **in-memory** file list, which is empty for a freshly constructed scratch log, so files left on disk are invisible to it.

So a round that is aborted after it started writing the scratch folder leaves that folder dirty and nothing ever notices:

- the round can be aborted by a broker restart or `kill -9` (the round is scheduled in the background; `CompactionStore.shutdown` waits 1 s and then calls `shutdownNow`), or by any exception inside the round — `compactAndReplace` has no `finally` and `doCompaction` swallows the throwable.

The next round then corrupts the live compaction log, because the scratch file name is reused:

1. the new scratch `MappedFileQueue` starts empty, so the first append creates/opens the same file name (`…/compacting/00000000000000000000`) — `MappedFileQueue.tryCreateMappedFile` constructs a `DefaultMappedFile` over the existing path, which opens it `rw` and maps it **without truncating** and with `wrotePosition = 0`;
2. the new content overwrites the file from offset 0 and `putEndMessage(compacting.getLog())` (`:674-679`) declares the file full;
3. whatever the aborted round had written beyond the new content is still there, and `replaceFiles` / `replaceCqFiles` (`:707`, `:755`) move that file into the live compaction log / consume queue.

The result is a compacted view that contains records from two rounds mixed together (with offsets from the aborted round), i.e. duplicated or stale messages for the compaction topic, and a consume queue whose tail does not belong to the log content.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a topic with the compaction attribute and let a compaction round run (or force one) until it has written into `<compactionLogPath>/<topic>/<queueId>/compacting/`.
2. Abort the round before it finishes the replace step (restart the broker, `kill -9`, or make it throw) — the scratch folder keeps its files.
3. Let the next round run: it reopens the same scratch file and appends the new compacted content on top of the old bytes, then moves it into the live log.

At the unit level the defect is proven with the existing `CompactionLogTest` harness (no RocksDB involved): pre-create `…/<topic>/<queueId>/compacting/00000000000000000000` as a leftover, run `compaction(...)` with `putEndMessage` stubbed, and observe that the leftover file still exists afterwards — verified today with `assertFalse("a scratch file left by an interrupted round must not survive into the next round", leftover.exists())`, which fails.

### What Did You Expect to See?

A scratch folder that is guaranteed to be empty when a round starts — the same guarantee `TopicPartitionLog.clean(...)` is written to check after a round. With that, an aborted round can at worst lose the messages it was compacting (they are re-compacted by the next round) instead of mixing its output into the live log.

### What Did You See Instead?

The leftover files of the aborted round are silently reused and their stale bytes end up inside the live compaction log / consume queue, so consumers of the compaction topic can see duplicated or stale records.

### Additional Context

Minimal fix: empty the scratch sub-folder right after the scratch log is constructed, for both scratch folders that follow this pattern (`COMPACTING_SUB_FOLDER` in `compaction(...)`, `REPLICATING_SUB_FOLDER` in `pullMessageFromMaster(...)`, `:202`), by deleting the two scratch store paths (`scratch.getLog().getStorePath()` and `scratch.getCQ().getMappedFileQueue().getStorePath()`). Clean rounds are unaffected — the folders are empty then, and the existing post-round `clean(...)` check keeps working.

I will open a PR with that change plus the regression test above (red before: the leftover survives the round; green after: the scratch folder is emptied before the round writes into it).

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I have searched the [open issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.
- [x] This is a defect in Apache RocketMQ, not a usage question.
- [x] I can reproduce this on the current `develop` branch.

### RocketMQ Version

develop @ `5d68880cbdfa5c6d87b5681c5eb3684df0e18ef8` (the revision this was verified on)

### Describe the Bug

`mqadmin createUser -p <secret>` and `mqadmin updateUser -p <secret>` run the password through `StringUtils.trim` before calling the admin API:

```java
String username = StringUtils.trim(commandLine.getOptionValue('u'));
String password = StringUtils.trim(commandLine.getOptionValue('p'));   // <-- the secret
String userType = StringUtils.trim(commandLine.getOptionValue('t'));
```

A secret is a payload, not a name. RocketMQ stores the secret it is given (`AuthMigrator` copies `accessConfig.getSecretKey()` into the user record, `User.of(accessKey, secretKey, ...)` in the authentication manager) and every client is authenticated against exactly that string, so leading or trailing whitespace is part of a legal secret - and secrets pasted from a vault or a file routinely carry one.

The CLI silently stores the trimmed value, so:

- `mqadmin createUser -u bob -p "  s3cret  " -b 127.0.0.1:10911` stores `s3cret`;
- every client that presents the real secret `"  s3cret  "` is rejected as unauthenticated, and nothing in the CLI output or the broker log points at the difference;
- through the admin API the same secret is stored verbatim, so the CLI and the API disagree about the same user.

The neighbouring command `sendMessage` carried the same shape for the message body until #11414 dropped its `.trim()`.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `mqadmin createUser -u bob -p "  s3cret  " -b 127.0.0.1:10911` (or the same through `updateUser`).
2. Read the stored user back (`mqadmin getUser -u bob -b 127.0.0.1:10911`): the stored secret is `s3cret`, not the string that was passed.
3. Authenticate one client with `"  s3cret  "` and one with `s3cret`: the first is rejected, the second succeeds.

A unit test makes the same point without a broker: the mocked `DefaultMQAdminExt` receives `"s3cret"` for the argument `"  s3cret  "`:

```
CreateUserSubCommandTest.testCreateKeepsThePasswordVerbatim:65 expected:<[  s3cret  ]> but was:<[s3cret]>
UpdateUserSubCommandTest.testUpdateKeepsThePasswordVerbatim:65 expected:<[ p@ss word ]> but was:<[p@ss word]>
```

### What Did You Expect to See?

The password reaches `createUser` / `updateUser` exactly as the operator passed it. The username, the user type and the broker address keep their trim.

### What Did You See Instead?

Both commands trim the secret, so a secret with leading or trailing whitespace cannot be provisioned through mqadmin at all, and the mismatch only shows up later as an authentication failure.

It mirrors the existing codec family exactly.

RocketMQ enforces a fixed 120-character subscription group limit to keep generated retry topics within 255 characters. Some broker integrations already guarantee that invariant but need longer group names, so otherwise valid groups cannot be created.

### Motivation
Allow broker operators to support longer subscription group names without changing the default behavior or relaxing client and gRPC validation globally.

### Describe the Solution You'd Like
Add a broker configuration for the subscription group name limit. Keep the default at 120, cap the effective value at 255, and apply it only to broker-side group creation paths. Callers that raise the limit remain responsible for keeping generated retry topics within 255 characters.

### Describe Alternatives You've Considered
Environment variables and JVM system properties have JVM-wide scope, require restart, and are not visible through broker configuration management. Raising the global default would weaken the existing retry-topic safeguard for all users.

### Additional Context
This is a follow-up improvement to #9563. Group names over 122 characters cannot use `%DLQ%<group>` because broker writes reject topics over 127 bytes; this proposal does not change that existing storage constraint.

### Search before asking

I checked open and closed issues and PRs for `AdminSendMessage`, `system_properties.keys`, `buildAdminMessage` and `setKeys`. The open work on this class (#11356 / PR #11357 on message-group queue selection, #11406 on retry-topic ACL) does not touch the message-key path, and no existing report covers the repeated keys field.

### What happened?

`AdminSendMessageRequest.system_properties.keys` is a repeated field, and the data plane keeps every entry: `SendMessageActivity` validates each key and calls `Message.setKeys(Collection)`, which joins the list. The admin surface does not. `ProxyAdminGrpcService.buildAdminMessage` reads the same field but keeps only the first non-empty entry:

```java
for (String key : systemProperties.getKeysList()) {
    if (!key.isEmpty()) {
        message.setKeys(key);
        break;
    }
}
```

Send a message through `AdminSendMessage` with `system_properties.keys = ["k1", "k2", "k3"]` and the stored message carries only `k1`. The RPC answers `OK` with a message id, so nothing tells the caller that two index keys vanished. Messages keyed this way are then only findable by `k1` in key-based queries, which is the whole point of sending keys.

The singular `key` field still works (covered by the existing `adminSendMessageCarriesTagsKeysAndPropertiesTest`); only the repeated `system_properties.keys` path is lossy.

### Runtime

develop at 57c2dc0, Temurin 11 (the pinned surefire/ByteBuddy stack does not run on JDK 21). Reproduced with the existing `ProxyAdminGrpcServiceTest` mocks — no broker needed. On the unpatched service, the new test fails with:

```text
expected:<key1[ key2 key3]> but was:<key1[]>
```

### Expected behavior

Every non-empty entry of `system_properties.keys` ends up on the message, space-joined like the data plane does. Empty entries are skipped. Precedence stays as it is today: a non-empty `system_properties.keys` overrides the singular `key`; an all-empty list leaves the singular key in place.

body_text:
### Search before asking

I checked open and closed issues and PRs for `ProxyAdminAuthInterceptor`, `METHOD_PERMISSIONS`, `proxy.admin` authorization and unmapped admin methods. The nearby open work is different: #11362 / PR #11363 changes which address the ACL is evaluated against, and #11178 / PR #11179 refuses to start when authorization is enabled without authentication. Neither covers what happens to a method that has no entry in the permission map.

### What happened?

`ProxyAdminAuthInterceptor` binds every admin RPC to a `proxy.admin.*` resource through the static `METHOD_PERMISSIONS` map. The authorization branch is guarded by `resourceAction != null`:

```java
ResourceAction resourceAction = METHOD_PERMISSIONS.get(method);
if (resourceAction != null && authzEnabled) {
    ... authorize against proxy.admin.<module> ...
}
return next.startCall(call, headers);   // unmapped methods land here
```

A method with no entry skips authorization completely and is served. With cluster authorization on, every *mapped* method gets a real ACL decision, but an unmapped one runs with authentication only — and the same is true in `grpcAdminServerAuthEnable` fail-closed mode, which only checks that authentication and authorization are *enabled*, not that this method is covered by them.

The admin server currently hosts only the `Admin` service and all 16 of its RPCs are mapped, so nothing is exploitable on develop today. But the surface grows from the rocketmq-apis side — the Admin service gained RPCs in three recent commits (#113, #115, #116) — and nothing cross-checks the proto against the map. The first future RPC merged without a hand-written entry becomes an authorization bypass by construction, including whatever mutation it introduces.

### Expected behavior

When the cluster authorization switch is on, a served method that has no `proxy.admin.*` mapping should be refused (the class already documents fail-closed as its behavior mode) rather than served without a permission check. The map and the served surface should also be pinned against each other in tests, so adding an RPC without deciding its resource and action fails CI instead of shipping a silent hole.

### Runtime

develop at 57c2dc0, JDK 11. Reproduced with the existing interceptor test harness — no broker or proxy required. On the current code, a call to an unmapped method name with `authorizationEnabled=true` reaches `next.startCall(...)`; the new test fails exactly there.

body_text:
### Search before asking

I checked open and closed issues and PRs for proxy admin metrics, OpenTelemetry on the control plane and admin gRPC instrumentation. What exists is adjacent, not this:

- #10901 / #10833 touch how metric config values are parsed (OTLP headers, colon-separated labels); #10950 masks them in config logs.
- #10603 (RIP-2) adds its own `ClientAdminMetricsRecorder` for the new client-admin query endpoint — service-level instrumentation for code that does not exist on develop yet.
- #10825 tracks the admin interface work in general.

Nothing records anything for the admin gRPC server that actually ships today: `ProxyAdminAuthInterceptor` answers every admin RPC (thread dumps, message verification, group resets, topic updates...) and `rocketmq_proxy_up` is the only proxy instrument in the pipeline.

### What happened?

`ProxyMetricsManager` initializes an OpenTelemetry meter in both proxy modes and exports it (OTLP/Prometheus/log), but the only instrument it registers is the `rocketmq_proxy_up` gauge. The admin gRPC server — the control plane surface every ops tool talks to — contributes no counter, no latency histogram, no error count.

So on a running proxy you cannot answer: is the admin interface being called at all, which methods are hot, how long do admin calls take, and — the important one — is anything failing (auth rejections, broken forwards, internal errors) while the dashboard still shows a healthy `rocketmq_proxy_up = 1`.

### Expected behavior

Each admin RPC should produce one count and one latency sample, labeled with the method name and terminal status code, exported through the proxy's existing OpenTelemetry pipeline alongside `rocketmq_proxy_up`. Calls rejected by the auth interceptor should be counted too (that is where failures would show up first), and everything should degrade to a no-op when metrics are disabled or the manager has not started — same idiom the broker uses for optional instruments.

### Runtime

develop at 57c2dc0, JDK 11. No proto change, no new dependency: the interceptor, the two instruments and tests live entirely in `proxy`.

### Search before asking

I checked open and closed issues and PRs for `TopicQueueMappingCleanService`, queue-mapping cleanup and static-topic null handling. #8728 (closed) asked for more unit tests on this service and is resolved; #8752 is an unrelated crash report. No open issue or PR covers a failed clean pass, and no open PR currently touches `TopicQueueMappingCleanService.java`.

### What happened?

`TopicQueueMappingCleanService.cleanItemListMoreThanSecondGen()` reconciles queue mappings after a leader move: for every queue whose leader moved away, it fetches the new leader's mapping and confirms the new leader really owns that queue. The check is:

```java
List<LogicQueueMappingItem> items = remoteMappingDetail.getHostedQueues().get(qId);
if (items.isEmpty()) {
    continue;
}
```

`getHostedQueues()` is a map, so when the remote broker's mapping has **no entry at all** for this queue id, `get(qId)` returns `null` and `items.isEmpty()` throws `NullPointerException`.

That "no entry" state is not hypothetical — it is precisely the transient inconsistency this service exists to reconcile (a mapping update that has not propagated to the new leader yet, or a leader that never hosted that queue). The NPE is caught by the per-topic `catch (Throwable)`, so the damage is silent:

- the current clean pass for that topic stops at the first such queue,
- every **remaining** queue of the same topic is skipped for this cycle (queues that would otherwise have been cleaned are not),
- the same failure repeats on the next 5-minute cycle, logging an error each time.

So one unpropagated queue can keep a whole topic's stale mapping entries alive indefinitely.

### Expected behavior

A remote mapping that does not contain the queue id should be treated like the other "not confirmed yet" cases nearby (`continue`), not crash the pass. The remaining queues of the topic must still be evaluated and cleaned in the same cycle.

### Runtime

develop at 57c2dc0, JDK 11. Reproduced against the existing `TopicQueueMappingCleanServiceTest` fixtures: a topic with two moved queues where the new leader's mapping omits one of them. With the current code the second queue is never removed; with a null guard it is removed in the same pass.

### Before Creating the Bug Report

- [x] I found a bug, not just asking a question, which should be created in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions).
- [x] I have searched the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/issues) and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq/discussions)  of this repository and believe that this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I have confirmed that this bug belongs to the current repository, not other repositories of RocketMQ.

### Runtime platform environment

Any (reproduced on macOS)

### RocketMQ version

develop, git commit id: 57c2dc04f78cc7e73e6b8c9436ee0fff0d0f46c3

### JDK Version

JDK 17

### Describe the Bug

`NettyRemotingClient#getProxy` picks a SOCKS proxy by matching the target host against each CIDR key of `socksProxyConfig`. For every key other than the literal `0.0.0.0/0` it calls `RemotingHelper#ipInCIDR(host, cidr)`, which parses the host with `ipToInt` and only accepts dotted IPv4 literals.

When the target address uses a hostname (e.g. `namesrv.example.com:9876`, common with Kubernetes service names) or an IPv6 literal, `ipToInt` throws `NumberFormatException`. The exception escapes `getProxy` → `fetchBootstrap` → `doConnect`, so the client cannot connect to that address at all, even though it should just not match that CIDR.

### Steps to Reproduce

```java
NettyClientConfig config = new NettyClientConfig();
config.setSocksProxyConfig("{\"10.0.0.0/8\":{\"addr\":\"127.0.0.1:1080\"}}");
NettyRemotingClient client = new NettyRemotingClient(config);
// any invoke against "namesrv.example.com:9876" reaches getProxy(...)
```

Calling `getProxy("namesrv.example.com:9876")` (e.g. via reflection) throws:

```
java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "namesrv"
	at org.apache.rocketmq.remoting.common.RemotingHelper.ipToInt(RemotingHelper.java)
	at org.apache.rocketmq.remoting.common.RemotingHelper.ipInCIDR(RemotingHelper.java)
	at org.apache.rocketmq.remoting.netty.NettyRemotingClient.getProxy(NettyRemotingClient.java)
```

### What Did You Expect to See?

A hostname or IPv6 host that cannot be compared against an IPv4 CIDR does not match that entry (no proxy, direct connection), and can still match the `0.0.0.0/0` catch-all entry.

### What Did You See Instead?

`NumberFormatException` is thrown and the connection attempt fails.

### Additional Context

This is separate from #11068, which fixes the `/0` mask computation inside `ipInCIDR`. The fix proposed here only touches `NettyRemotingClient#getProxy`, so the two changes do not overlap.

### What happened

Zeta's job-scheduling completion path can permanently hang the single thread (`pending-job-schedule-runner`) that services **all** job scheduling for a master node. When it hangs, the triggering job never resolves past `JobStatus.UNKNOWABLE` (it never reaches a stable `FAILED` with a history record), and — because scheduling for every subsequent job submission on that master also runs through this same thread — the cluster's ability to schedule new jobs may be silently frozen from that point on, with no exception thrown and no error logged.

This was found while building an E2E regression test for an unrelated scenario (multi-pipeline restore contention after a worker is killed); the reproduction below is a side effect of that test's own setup phase, before its actual scenario ever runs.

### Root cause (traced from source + real CI logs, not yet confirmed with a live thread dump — see "what's still needed" below)

`CoordinatorService.completeFailJob()` (`seatunnel-engine/seatunnel-engine-server/src/main/java/org/apache/seatunnel/engine/server/CoordinatorService.java:510-525`) blocks on `jobMaster.getJobMasterCompleteFuture().join()` (line 520). The entire completion chain feeding that future runs **synchronously on the calling thread** — there is no executor hop anywhere in it:

- `PhysicalPlan.completeJobEndFuture()` (`PhysicalPlan.java:441-443`) calls `jobEndFuture.complete(...)` directly.
- `org.apache.seatunnel.engine.common.utils.concurrent.CompletableFuture.whenComplete()` (`CompletableFuture.java:102-104`) and `PassiveCompletableFuture`'s constructor (`PassiveCompletableFuture.java:30-41`) both use plain (non-`Async`) `whenComplete`, so the listener chain fires synchronously.
- This synchronously drives `JobMaster.initStateFuture()`'s completion callback (`JobMaster.java:488-497`), which calls `cleanJob()` (`JobMaster.java:966-971`) before completing `jobMasterCompleteFuture`.

`cleanJob()`'s steps include `checkpointManager.clearCheckpointIfNeed()`, `getJobDAGInfo()` (`JobMaster.java:856-877`, guarded by `synchronized(this)` — the **same monitor** used by `cancelJob()`/`stopJob()`), `jobHistoryService.storeJobInfo()`/`storeFinishedJobState()` (the actual `finishedJobStateImap.put()`, `JobHistoryService.java:257-261`), and `scheduleRemoveJobStateMaps()` (`JobMaster.java:825-838`, a synchronous `pendingJobCleanupIMap.put()`).

**If any single step inside `cleanJob()` blocks instead of returning, `jobMasterCompleteFuture` never completes, `completeFailJob()`'s `.join()` blocks forever, and the calling thread — `pending-job-schedule-runner`, the only thread that runs `CoordinatorService.pendingJobSchedule()` — is wedged permanently.**

This is a `REJECT`-schedule-strategy path specifically: a job whose `preApplyResources()` gets only a partial slot grant fails immediately and terminally under `REJECT` (`CoordinatorService.java:463` → `:510`), with no retry (contrast `WAIT`, which sleeps and requeues). This is the engine's config-file default strategy.

### Evidence (fork `davidzollo/seatunnel`, Actions run `34181138685`, job `101921574204`, JDK 11)

Job id `1149543734560423937` needed 12 of 16 total fixed slots across 2 workers; `preApplyResources()` got a partial grant (5 of 12 succeeded). Its complete log footprint (18 lines total) ends at `03:16:23.9357504Z`, immediately after the second `updateJobState(FAILED)` call inside `completeFailJob()`. **`completeFailJob()`'s own final log statement — `"The job %s is not running because the resources is not enough insufficient"` (`CoordinatorService.java:521-524`), reachable only *after* `.join()` returns — never appears for this job anywhere in the (315,221-line) log.**

Three sibling jobs failed via the identical REJECT path in the same run (`1149552276294074369`, `1149552325602312193`, `1149552375816519681`) and **do** show that final log line — i.e. `.join()` returned normally for them. Something specific to job `1149543734560423937` (plausibly its unusually large 12-slot/multi-pipeline fan-out, or a timing overlap with a concurrent operation on the same `JobMaster`) caused its `cleanJob()` to hang where the siblings' did not.

Ruled out as causes: an escaped `Throwable` on the scheduler thread (`CoordinatorService.java:323`'s `"Error in pending job schedule thread"` never appears near the incident); Hazelcast's own callback-exception-swallowing wrapper (`ExceptionUtil.withTryCatch`'s `"Exception during callback"` string appears 14 times elsewhere in this same log — confirming the mechanism is live and working — but zero times for this job); a lost/reordered IMap write (the relevant maps are the same object references throughout, no evidence of desync); stale `PeekBlockingQueue` bookkeeping (read in full, no bug found).

### Blast radius

If confirmed, this is not just "one job's status becomes unqueryable." Because `cleanJob()` runs on the shared, single `pending-job-schedule-runner` thread, a hang here could silently freeze scheduling for **every subsequent job submitted to that master**, with no crash, no exception, and no error logged anywhere — an operator would only notice new jobs never starting, with no obvious cause in the logs.

### Two candidate blocking points (not yet distinguished)

1. `getJobDAGInfo()`'s `synchronized(this)` (`JobMaster.java:856-877`) contending indefinitely with a concurrent `cancelJob()`/`stopJob()` holding the same monitor on the same `JobMaster` instance.
2. A stalled Hazelcast IMap operation — either the `finishedJobStateImap.put()` in `storeFinishedJobState()`, or a per-vertex `runningJobStateIMap.get()` loop inside whatever builds the job's DAG/state summary — potentially exposed specifically by this job's large fan-out (12 slots / multiple pipelines), which would make this a scale-dependent trigger rather than a purely random one.

### What's still needed to close this out

A thread dump (`jstack`) of the master JVM captured while `pending-job-schedule-runner` is confirmed wedged, during a live reproduction. Static/log analysis alone cannot distinguish between the two candidates above. The E2E test that originally surfaced this (`SplitClusterFaultToleranceIT#testManyPipelinesRestoreContentionInWorkerDown`, from PR #12109 — a 4-pipeline, 12-slot job submitted against a 2-worker/16-slot fixed-pool cluster under the default `REJECT` strategy) is a plausible starting point for reproduction, though it did not hang on every run (3 sibling jobs completed the same failure path normally in the same CI run), suggesting the trigger condition is timing-sensitive rather than deterministic on every partial-grant failure.

### Fix containment (once the exact blocking call is known)

Expected to be narrow: a bounded timeout around `cleanJob()`'s blocking calls (or around the `.join()` in `completeFailJob()` itself, with a fallback status write on timeout), confined to `CoordinatorService.java` and/or `JobMaster.java`. No architectural change anticipated — but this should not be assumed without confirming the actual blocking call first, since a timeout alone would mask the symptom without fixing whatever is actually stalling (e.g. real lock contention that could still starve other work).

Its complete log footprint (18 lines total) ends at `03:16:23.9357504Z`, immediately after the second `updateJobState(FAILED)` call inside `completeFailJob()`. **`completeFailJob()`'s own final log statement — `"The job %s is not running because the resources is not enough insufficient"` (`CoordinatorService.java:521-524`), reachable only *after* `.join()` returns — never appears for this job anywhere in the (315,221-line) log.**

Three sibling jobs failed via the identical REJECT path in the same run (`1149552276294074369`, `1149552325602312193`, `1149552375816519681`) and **do** show that final log line — i.e. `.join()` returned normally for them. Something specific to job `1149543734560423937` (plausibly its unusually large 12-slot/multi-pipeline fan-out, or a timing overlap with a concurrent operation on the same `JobMaster`) caused its `cleanJob()` to hang where the siblings' did not.

Ruled out as causes: an escaped `Throwable` on the scheduler thread (`CoordinatorService.java:323`'s `"Error in pending job schedule thread"` never appears near the incident); Hazelcast's own callback-exception-swallowing wrapper (`ExceptionUtil.withTryCatch`'s `"Exception during callback"` string appears 14 times elsewhere in this same log — confirming the mechanism is live and working — but zero times for this job); a lost/reordered IMap write (the relevant maps are the same object references throughout, no evidence of desync); stale `PeekBlockingQueue` bookkeeping (read in full, no bug found).

### Blast radius

If confirmed, this is not just "one job's status becomes unqueryable." Because `cleanJob()` runs on the shared, single `pending-job-schedule-runner` thread, a hang here could silently freeze scheduling for **every subsequent job submitted to that master**, with no crash, no exception, and no error logged anywhere — an operator would only notice new jobs never starting, with no obvious cause in the logs.

### Two candidate blocking points (not yet distinguished)

1. `getJobDAGInfo()`'s `synchronized(this)` (`JobMaster.java:856-877`) contending indefinitely with a concurrent `cancelJob()`/`stopJob()` holding the same monitor on the same `JobMaster` instance.
2. A stalled Hazelcast IMap operation — either the `finishedJobStateImap.put()` in `storeFinishedJobState()`, or a per-vertex `runningJobStateIMap.get()` loop inside whatever builds the job's DAG/state summary — potentially exposed specifically by this job's large fan-out (12 slots / multiple pipelines), which would make this a scale-dependent trigger rather than a purely random one.

### What's still needed to close this out

A thread dump (`jstack`) of the master JVM captured while `pending-job-schedule-runner` is confirmed wedged, during a live reproduction. Static/log analysis alone cannot distinguish between the two candidates above. The E2E test that originally surfaced this (`SplitClusterFaultToleranceIT#testManyPipelinesRestoreContentionInWorkerDown`, from PR #12109 — a 4-pipeline, 12-slot job submitted against a 2-worker/16-slot fixed-pool cluster under the default `REJECT` strategy) is a plausible starting point for reproduction, though it did not hang on every run (3 sibling jobs completed the same failure path normally in the same CI run), suggesting the trigger condition is timing-sensitive rather than deterministic on every partial-grant failure.

### Fix containment (once the exact blocking call is known)

Expected to be narrow: a bounded timeout around `cleanJob()`'s blocking calls (or around the `.join()` in `completeFailJob()` itself, with a fallback status write on timeout), confined to `CoordinatorService.java` and/or `JobMaster.java`. No architectural change anticipated — but this should not be assumed without confirming the actual blocking call first, since a timeout alone would mask the symptom without fixing whatever is actually stalling (e.g. real lock contention that could still starve other work).

Part of the umbrella #12207. This issue tracks the shared, engine-agnostic half of table-level lineage reporting: two new modules and the configuration surface both engines will use. No engine wiring here — see #12205 (Zeta) and #12206 (Flink).

### What's needed

- `seatunnel-lineage`: configuration resolution with job/environment/cluster precedence, the `LineageEvent`/`LineageDataset`/`LineageEventType` model, dataset naming per the OpenLineage naming spec, and a `LineageBackend` SPI (`ServiceLoader`-based, not SeaTunnel's existing `EventHandler` SPI — that one broadcasts to a shared event stream that already has a default subscriber, which would leak custom lineage properties into unrelated logs).
- `seatunnel-lineage-openlineage`: the default `LineageBackend` — OpenLineage 1.29.0 model classes (`io.openlineage:openlineage-java`, model classes only) plus a hand-written `httpclient 4.5.13`-based transport.
- 11 new `env {}` options, all prefixed `openlineage_` (`openlineage_enabled`, `_transport`, `_url`, `_namespace`, `_auth_token`, `_timeout_ms`, `_retry_times`, `_run_facet`, `_run_properties`, `_heartbeat_min_interval_ms`, `_producer`). All optional; `openlineage_enabled` defaults to `false`.

### Notable constraints this issue needs to satisfy

- **Token handling**: `openlineage_auth_token` must be rejected if it appears in a job's `env {}` block. Job configuration can be persisted to disk or serialized into a Flink `JobGraph` (which lands in HA storage / the BlobServer) — the token may only come from a process environment variable or cluster-level configuration, resolved at execution time, never at parse time.
- **Serialization safety**: SeaTunnel's existing shaded `ObjectMapper` cannot be reused to serialize OpenLineage's model classes — they rely on `@JsonAnyGetter` for custom facet properties, and the shaded Jackson silently produces a corrupted event (the facet gets wrapped in a literal `additionalProperties` key instead of having its properties inlined) with no error raised. The new modules therefore ship their own unshaded Jackson, isolated by module boundary.
- **Dependency footprint**: pulling in `openlineage-java` unfiltered adds ~13 redundant transitive jars and a `commons-logging`/`org.slf4j:jcl-over-slf4j` duplicate-class conflict. Needs 4 explicit Maven `<exclusion>`s (`httpclient5`, `micrometer-core`, `commons-logging`, `commons-lang3`) while keeping the YAML/Jackson dependencies OpenLineage's own static initializers need.
- **License/dependency bookkeeping**: register the new runtime jar in `tools/dependencies/known-dependencies.txt` and `seatunnel-dist/release-docs/LICENSE`; make sure `httpcore` doesn't end up at two different versions in the distribution (pin to the version the rest of the repo already ships).

### Backward compatibility

Purely additive. No existing option, module, or SPI is touched.

body_text:
Part of the umbrella #12207, depends on #12204 (the shared `seatunnel-lineage`/`seatunnel-lineage-openlineage` modules). Adds the Zeta engine's call site.

### What's needed

A `ZetaLineageReporter`, wired from the job master (`JobMaster` / `PhysicalPlan` / `CheckpointCoordinator`), that when `openlineage_enabled = true`:

- Sends a START event when a job's pipeline begins.
- Sends a throttled RUNNING heartbeat on completed checkpoints, so long-running streaming jobs don't go stale in a lineage graph — throttled by `openlineage_heartbeat_min_interval_ms` (default 1 hour) since checkpoints can complete every few seconds and Zeta has no other natural place to hang a periodic callback.
- Sends a terminal COMPLETE/FAIL/ABORT event when the pipeline ends, with output row-count/byte-size statistics read from the job's own `SinkCommittedCount`/`SinkWriteCount` metrics (falling back to the "attempted" counts if nothing has committed yet, flagged with an `output_statistics_semantics` facet so a consumer of the event knows which one it's looking at — Zeta and Flink end up reporting structurally different semantics here, and both need to say so rather than silently disagreeing).
- Splits a multi-table sink's event into one event per underlying table, and derives each table's OpenLineage dataset name from its `CatalogTable` per the shared naming logic in #12204.

### Backward compatibility

Reporting is off unless a job explicitly sets `openlineage_enabled = true`. No change to checkpoint behavior, job scheduling, or existing metrics when disabled.

Part of the umbrella #12207, depends on #12204 (the shared `seatunnel-lineage`/`seatunnel-lineage-openlineage` modules). Adds the Flink engine's call site — `seatunnel-flink-20-starter` only.

### What's needed

- A `seatunnel-lineage-flink` module holding `LineageJobStatusHook`, which implements Flink's `org.apache.flink.core.execution.JobStatusHook` — a Flink 1.16+ API, which is why this is a separate module rather than living in `seatunnel-flink-starter-common`: a module compiled against Flink 1.13/1.15 can't even name the interface. The 13/15 starters simply don't get lineage reporting; this is a documented limitation, not a bug to fix here.
- Client-side registration (`FlinkLineageHooks`/`FlinkLineageSupport` in the 20-starter and the common starter module) that builds the START event, registers the hook on the `StreamGraph`, and — for an **attached** submission (`flink run` without `-d`) — reports the COMPLETE event itself once `execute()` returns, because only the client can read Flink's job accumulators for the real row/byte counts. For a **detached** submission (`-d`), no client is left around by the time the job finishes, so the JobManager-side hook reports the terminal event itself, without statistics. Both paths must agree on exactly one terminal event; whichever one runs must tell the other to stay silent.
- The hook's terminal-event send must not run inline on Flink's job-status-change callback — that callback is on a thread Flink's own scheduling depends on, and a slow or stuck HTTP call there is a self-inflicted latency problem. The send needs to be handed off to its own executor.
- 🔒 The auth token must never be serialized into the `JobStatusHook` instance — that instance is serialized into the `JobGraph`, which lands in Flink's HA storage / BlobServer. The hook must re-resolve the token from the JobManager's own environment or cluster configuration at execution time.
- Deployment documentation: because `JobGraph` deserialization on the JobManager happens *before* the user classloader exists, the hook's implementation class must already be on the JobManager's system classpath — a shaded uber-jar needs to be placed in `$FLINK_HOME/lib` and the JobManager restarted. The client-side starter jar and the cluster-side shaded jar are two different artifacts and must be upgraded together: a version mismatch doesn't error, it silently falls back to older behavior (Java serialization gives a missing field its default value rather than throwing).

### Backward compatibility

Reporting is off unless a job explicitly sets `openlineage_enabled = true`. Nothing changes for Flink 1.13/1.15 users, since those starters don't carry this code at all.

body_text:
### Motivation

Metadata/lineage platforms that speak [OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io/) (Marquez, Gravitino, DataHub, ...) have no way to learn which tables a SeaTunnel job read from and wrote to. This is an umbrella issue for adding opt-in, table-level lineage reporting so a SeaTunnel job can tell such a receiver, in the standard OpenLineage `RunEvent` shape, what it ran and what it touched.

### What this adds

- A START event when a job (or one of its pipelines) begins, a terminal COMPLETE/FAIL/ABORT event when it ends, and an optional throttled RUNNING heartbeat for long-running streaming jobs.
- Table-level datasets only (no column-level lineage), named per the OpenLineage naming spec.
- Output row-count/byte-size statistics on the terminal event where the engine can obtain them.
- Everything here is **off by default** and fully opt-in via a new `openlineage_enabled` job option.

### Scope

- Engines: **Zeta** and the **Flink 1.20 starter**. Spark and the Flink 13/15 starters are explicitly out of scope (the latter two because `JobStatusHook`, the hook this design relies on, is a Flink 1.16+ API).
- Granularity: table-level only. Column-level lineage would require per-transform field-mapping resolution (including SQL lineage parsing for the `Sql` transform) and is a separate, larger effort.

### Design

Two small new modules carry the engine-agnostic pieces, so neither engine's code needs to know about OpenLineage directly:

- `seatunnel-lineage`: configuration resolution (11 new `openlineage_*` job options), the `LineageEvent`/`LineageDataset` model, dataset naming per the OpenLineage spec, and a pluggable `LineageBackend` SPI.
- `seatunnel-lineage-openlineage`: the default backend — OpenLineage 1.29.0 model classes plus a hand-rolled `httpclient`-based transport (neither `openlineage-java`'s own transport nor SeaTunnel's existing shaded Jackson infrastructure could be reused as-is; see PR #12208 for why).

Each engine gets a thin call site on top of that:

- Zeta: `ZetaLineageReporter`, invoked from the job master.
- Flink (1.20 starter only): `LineageJobStatusHook` (JobManager-side, implements Flink's `JobStatusHook`) plus a client-side registration/statistics path, because attached and detached Flink submissions need different terminal-event handling.

### PR plan

Split into 3 PRs, each based on `dev`, to keep each review scope narrow:

1. **PR #12208**: the two new modules, config options, dependency/license bookkeeping. No engine wiring. Implements #12204.
2. **PR #12209**: the Zeta call site. Built on top of #12208's branch, so its diff includes #12208's changes until that one merges — see the PR description for the exact commit range to review. Implements #12205.

### What this adds

- A START event when a job (or one of its pipelines) begins, a terminal COMPLETE/FAIL/ABORT event when it ends, and an optional throttled RUNNING heartbeat for long-running streaming jobs.
- Table-level datasets only (no column-level lineage), named per the OpenLineage naming spec.
- Output row-count/byte-size statistics on the terminal event where the engine can obtain them.
- Everything here is **off by default** and fully opt-in via a new `openlineage_enabled` job option.

### Scope

- Engines: **Zeta** and the **Flink 1.20 starter**. Spark and the Flink 13/15 starters are explicitly out of scope (the latter two because `JobStatusHook`, the hook this design relies on, is a Flink 1.16+ API).

body_text:
## Description

Follow-up from #12156 review (F2). Not a regression report; the race is pre-existing.

Verified at `dev` commit `4c25d9a62c68f9a7e13e404c1a81b3a3c56886de` (the #12156 head, after that PR replaced the ordinal range checks):

- `PhysicalPlan.cancelJob()` and `PhysicalPlan.stopJob()` evaluate `NOT_STARTED_STATUSES.contains(jobStatus)` and then call `updateJobState(...)` as two separate steps.
- `updateJobState` (`PhysicalPlan.java:323`) is `synchronized` on the `PhysicalPlan` instance, and so are `startJob()` (`:379`) and `stateProcess()` (`:391`).
- The not-started check is *outside* that monitor, so a job can move from `PENDING`/`CREATED`/`INITIALIZING` to `SCHEDULED`/`RUNNING` between the check and the transition. In that window `cancelJob()` would take the `CANCELED` shortcut for a job that has just started, skipping the `CANCELING` drain path.

## Why it was not folded into #12156

Moving the check under the `updateJobState` monitor changes lock ordering with `startJob()`/`stateProcess()`, rather than just relocating a condition. That deserves its own review, so #12156 deliberately kept its diff to the ordinal-check replacement plus tests and documentation.

## Expected outcome

- Decide whether the not-started check should be evaluated under the same monitor as the transition it guards (a `synchronized` helper on `PhysicalPlan`, or a single method owning both steps), or whether the race is unreachable in practice — in which case it should be stated why, with a test that pins it.
- If the check moves under the monitor, keep the `NOT_STARTED_STATUSES` semantics from #12156 unchanged: a job in `INITIALIZING`/`CREATED`/`PENDING` goes straight to `CANCELED` with no `CANCELING` transition.
- Add regression coverage for the interleaving, not just the two static outcomes: the existing tests in `StateTransitionCleanupTest` assert the classification for a quiescent job and cannot observe a check-then-act race.

## Related

- PR: #12156 (adds `NOT_STARTED_STATUSES`, `PhysicalPlan`-level cancel tests)
- Review thread: #12156 comment on F2
