body_text:
### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22bug%22) and found no similar issues.


### What happened

When checkpointing is on, the JDBC sink commits only at checkpoint time (prepareCommit), on a timer flush, or on close. If the connection uses manual commit (auto_commit = false, or Oracle, which the sink always switches to manual commit), every batch-size flush between two commits goes into the same open transaction.

If that transaction is lost before the commit, the earlier flushed batches are gone. The sink does not notice, and the next checkpoint still succeeds. I found two ways this happens.

1. Flush retry (needs max_retries > 0)

Batch A is flushed into the open transaction, but not committed yet.
The flush of batch B fails. Either the connection drops (SQLState 08xxx), or the database rolls back the whole transaction (SQLState 40001, for example a deadlock).
JdbcOutputFormat.flush reconnects if needed and retries. The retry only re-sends batch B, because batch A was already cleared from the executor buffer after its own successful flush.
The checkpoint commits. Only batch B is in the database. Batch A is lost, and there is no error.

2. Pooled connection replaced before commit (default config)

ConnectionPoolManager.getConnection(index) silently replaces a cached connection that is no longer usable. In Zeta every JDBC sink runs through MultiTableSink, even with a single table, so this pool is the normal path.

Batches are flushed into the open transaction on connection C1.
C1 dies before the checkpoint, for example from a network blip, a DB failover, or an idle timeout. The database rolls back its transaction.
In prepareCommit, commitIfNeeded() calls connectionProvider.getConnection(), gets a new connection C2, and commits it. C2 has nothing to commit, so the commit succeeds and the checkpoint succeeds.
Everything flushed on C1 since the last checkpoint is lost, and there is no error.

In both cases the rows are not replayed. The checkpoint succeeded, so the source offsets moved past them.

With auto_commit = true (the default for most databases) each batch is committed by the driver right away, so neither path loses data.

### SeaTunnel Version

dev (checked at af80a6704be4734b20a913f46f3838c3770688eb)

### SeaTunnel Config

```conf
env {
  parallelism = 1
  job.mode = "STREAMING"
  checkpoint.interval = 60000
}

source {
  # any source
}

sink {
  Jdbc {
    url = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/test"
    driver = "org.postgresql.Driver"
    user = "postgres"
    password = "postgres"
    database = "test"
    table = "public.t"
    generate_sink_sql = true
    primary_keys = ["id"]
    auto_commit = false
    batch_size = 1000
    max_retries = 3   # path 1 only; path 2 also happens with the default 0
  }
}
```

### Running Command

```shell
./bin/seatunnel.sh --config jdbc_sink.conf -m local

To trigger it, kill the sink's database session after the first batch flush and before the next checkpoint. On Postgres you can find it in pg_stat_activity (state idle in transaction) and end it with pg_terminate_backend(pid).
```

### Error Exception

```log
None. That is the problem: the job keeps running and the checkpoint succeeds.
With max_retries > 0 the only trace is one "JDBC executeBatch error, retry times = 0" ERROR line, followed by a successful retry.
```

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Zeta (dev)

### Java or Scala Version

1.8

### Screenshots

Deterministic reproduction with SQLite (no Docker needed). Both tests fail on dev, because the checkpoint succeeds and rows are lost:

JdbcMultiTableReconnectTest#manualCommitWriterDoesNotDropEarlierBatchWhenLaterBatchReconnects: path 1.
JdbcMultiTableReconnectTest#manualCommitWriterFailsCheckpointWhenConnectionIsReplacedBeforeCommit: path 2. The test provider swaps a dead connection on getConnection(), the same way ConnectionPoolManager does.

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [feature](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22Feature%22) and found no similar feature requirement.

### Description

When a Zeta job is not making progress, `seatunnel-cli` has nothing to say about it. The only way to find out why is to read the server log, which means getting onto the master node -- and the two most common answers are already in the REST API before anyone opens a log file.

`/job-info/<id>` has carried a `diagnostics` block since #11982/#11983/#11984: per-state entry timestamps at both job and pipeline level, plus each pipeline's restore counter and its limit. That is enough to answer, by arithmetic rather than by guessing:

- **"it says RUNNING but nothing is moving"** -- a pipeline is failing and being restored in a loop, visible as `restoreCount` climbing toward `maxRestoreCount`. The job status stays RUNNING the whole time, which is exactly why this one is hard to spot by hand.
- **"it has been stuck for ages"** -- how long ago the job entered its current state. A job sitting in SCHEDULED usually means the cluster could not grant the slots it asked for; a job sitting in CANCELING means a task is ignoring the stop request. Those are different problems and currently look identical from outside.
- **"it ran but the target is empty"** -- `SourceReceivedCount` and `SinkWriteCount` say whether rows were read at all, and whether they were dropped between source and sink.
- **a failed job's actual cause** -- `errorMsg` already goes through `parse_error` (#12535) elsewhere in the CLI, so the error code and innermost `Caused by` can be surfaced directly instead of a wall of stack trace.

### Proposal

`seatunnel --diagnose <jobId>`: fetch `/job-info/<jobId>`, apply deterministic rules to it, print what matched.

Three properties worth fixing in the design rather than leaving to chance:

1. **No model.** These conclusions are derived, not inferred -- a restore count of 7 is a crash loop whatever a model thinks. Keeping it model-free also means it works with no API key and no provider configured, which is the state a lot of operators are in when something breaks at 3am.
2. **Read-only.** One GET. No submit, no stop, no savepoint. That is what makes it safe to point at a live production job.
3. **Non-zero exit only for a genuinely failed job.** A stuck or crash-looping job is still a live job; exiting non-zero for it would break `seatunnel --diagnose x && ...` for a job that is merely slow.

An LLM explanation on top of the same evidence, and a diagnostics tool the conversational agent can call when asked about a job, are both natural follow-ups -- but they belong on top of this, not instead of it.

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [X] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

- [X] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://www.apache.org/foundation/policies/conduct)

body_text:
### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22bug%22) and found no similar issues.

### What happened

An arrow IPC stream may carry more than one record batch, and `ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader` is written to handle that: `readArrow` loops on `loadNextBatch()`, appends each batch's rows to a cumulative list, and accumulates `readRowCount`. The conversion step does not follow the same convention, so **every record batch after the first throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException`**.

**What I verified and what I did not.**

Verified, on `dev` at `11e4f5554`, by running it: the throw and the exact line it comes from; which batch shapes break and which do not, measured across 11 shapes; that both halves of the fix are required; and that after the fix the rows come back complete and in order, including a multi-column case with an `ARRAY` column and a `TIMESTAMP` column.

Not verified: whether a Doris or StarRocks backend actually packs more than one record batch into a single `TScanBatchResult`. That is a backend implementation detail I cannot establish from this repository, and no issue reports this crash. **So this is a report that the multi-batch code path is broken and untested, not a claim that Doris or StarRocks are crashing in production.**

### The defect

`ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.java:133-152`. Two indexing conventions are mixed in one loop:

```java
for (int i = 0; i < seatunnelRowBatch.size(); i++) {      // cumulative, across ALL batches
    if (fieldIndex != null) {
        ...
        Object fieldValue =
                convertArrowData(
                        readRowCount + i, minorType, fieldVector, seaTunnelDataType);   // indexes the VECTOR
        ...
        seatunnelRowBatch.get(readRowCount + i).setField(fieldIndex, fieldValue);       // indexes the LIST
    }
}
```

`seatunnelRowBatch` is cumulative, so `readRowCount + i` is right for it. `fieldVector` holds **only the batch currently loaded**, so indexing it by the absolute row number is wrong, and the loop bound is the cumulative size rather than this batch's row count.

With a first batch of 3 rows and a second of 4 (`readRowCount=3`, `size()=7`, this batch = 4):

| i | vector index `3+i` | list index `3+i` | outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 3, in range | 3 | writes the wrong row's value |
| 1,2,3 | 4,5,6 out of range | 4,5,6 | arrow returns null, no exception |
| 4 | | **7, size is 7** | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |

Measured stack:

```
java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 7 out of bounds for length 7
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList.get(ArrayList.java:459)
	at ...ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.convertSeatunnelRow(ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.java:148)
	at ...ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.readArrow(ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.java:111)
```

Note the throw comes from the `ArrayList`, not from arrow. Arrow answers an out-of-range index with `null` rather than an exception, which matters below.

### Which shapes break, measured

| batches | result |
| --- | --- |
| `{3}`, `{7}` single | correct |
| `{1,1}`, `{3,4}`, `{5,2}`, `{2,5}`, `{1,1,1}` | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| `{0,4}`, `{0,0,3}` leading empty batches | correct, they are skipped before `readRowCount` moves |
| `{4,0}` trailing empty | correct |
| `{4,0,2}` empty in the middle | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |

So the rule is: the first non-empty batch is handled correctly, and every later non-empty batch throws. It always throws, so no partially converted rows ever reach the caller on `dev` today.

### Why it has never been caught

Both tests in `ArrowToSeatunnelRowReaderTest` call `writer.writeBatch()` exactly once, `testSeatunnelRow` at `:316` and `testConvertArrowSpeed` at `:442`. A single batch makes `readRowCount` zero and `seatunnelRowBatch.size()` equal to this batch's row count, so both conventions coincide and the bug is invisible.

### A trap worth recording

The loop bound looks like the whole bug, and it is not. Correcting only the bound and leaving `readRowCount + i` on the vector removes the exception and replaces it with **silent data corruption**, because arrow returns `null` past the end instead of throwing. Measured, same 3+4 stream:

```
expected: <[0, 1, 2, 100, 101, 102, 103]>
but was:  <[0, 1, 2, 103, null, null, null]>
```

A regression test that asserts only the row count would pass against that. Any test for this needs to assert the values.

### Both halves are required

| change | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| neither (current `dev`) | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| loop bound only | no exception, wrong values as above |
| vector index only | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| both | correct |

### Fix

Bound the loop by the current batch's row count, and index the vector from 0 while continuing to index the cumulative list from `readRowCount`:

```java
for (int i = 0; i < rowCountInOneBatch; i++) {
    ...
    Object fieldValue = convertArrowData(i, minorType, fieldVector, seaTunnelDataType);
    ...
    seatunnelRowBatch.get(readRowCount + i).setField(fieldIndex, fieldValue);   // unchanged
}
```

Single-batch behaviour is unchanged by construction: with one batch `readRowCount` is 0 and `rowCountInOneBatch == seatunnelRowBatch.size()`, so both forms are identical. The existing tests, including the 1,000,000 row `testConvertArrowSpeed`, pass untouched.

Verified after the fix: all 11 shapes above return the right values in the right order, and a two-batch stream with `BIGINT`, `VARCHAR`, `ARRAY<INT>` and `TIMESTAMP` columns reads back all rows correctly, which exercises `ListConverter` and `TimeStampMilliConverter` through the changed `rowIndex`.

### Scope

`ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader` has two production callers, `DorisValueReader` and `StarRocksBeReadClient`, both passing `TScanBatchResult.getRows()` straight from the backend. As stated above, I make no claim about what those backends emit.

### SeaTunnel Version

`dev` at `11e4f5554`, 3.0.0-SNAPSHOT.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

- [X] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

{"repository": "apache/seatunnel", "task_candidate_id": 1175, "repository_id": 30, "issue_number": 12649, "github_issue_id": 5730737783, "html_url": "https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues/12649", "created_at": "2026-10-06T15:08:02+00:00", "author_association": "COLLABORATOR", "title": "[Bug][Connector-V2] ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader throws IndexOutOfBoundsException on any arrow stream with more than one record batch", "body_text": "### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22bug%22) and found no similar issues.

### What happened

An arrow IPC stream may carry more than one record batch, and `ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader` is written to handle that: `readArrow` loops on `loadNextBatch()`, appends each batch's rows to a cumulative list, and accumulates `readRowCount`. The conversion step does not follow the same convention, so **every record batch after the first throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException`**.

**What I verified and what I did not.**

Verified, on `dev` at `11e4f5554`, by running it: the throw and the exact line it comes from; which batch shapes break and which do not, measured across 11 shapes; that both halves of the fix are required; and that after the fix the rows come back complete and in order, including a multi-column case with an `ARRAY` column and a `TIMESTAMP` column.

Not verified: whether a Doris or StarRocks backend actually packs more than one record batch into a single `TScanBatchResult`. That is a backend implementation detail I cannot establish from this repository, and no issue reports this crash. **So this is a report that the multi-batch code path is broken and untested, not a claim that Doris or StarRocks are crashing in production.**

### The defect

`ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.java:133-152`. Two indexing conventions are mixed in one loop:

```java
for (int i = 0; i < seatunnelRowBatch.size(); i++) {      // cumulative, across ALL batches
    if (fieldIndex != null) {
        ...
        Object fieldValue =
                convertArrowData(
                        readRowCount + i, minorType, fieldVector, seaTunnelDataType);   // indexes the VECTOR
        ...
        seatunnelRowBatch.get(readRowCount + i).setField(fieldIndex, fieldValue);       // indexes the LIST
    }
}
```

`seatunnelRowBatch` is cumulative, so `readRowCount + i` is right for it. `fieldVector` holds **only the batch currently loaded**, so indexing it by the absolute row number is wrong, and the loop bound is the cumulative size rather than this batch's row count.

With a first batch of 3 rows and a second of 4 (`readRowCount=3`, `size()=7`, this batch = 4):

| i | vector index `3+i` | list index `3+i` | outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 3, in range | 3 | writes the wrong row's value |
| 1,2,3 | 4,5,6 out of range | 4,5,6 | arrow returns null, no exception |
| 4 | | **7, size is 7** | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |

Measured stack:

```
java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 7 out of bounds for length 7
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList.get(ArrayList.java:459)
	at ...ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.convertSeatunnelRow(ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.java:148)
	at ...ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.readArrow(ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader.java:111)
```

Note the throw comes from the `ArrayList`, not from arrow. Arrow answers an out-of-range index with `null` rather than an exception, which matters below.

### Which shapes break, measured

| batches | result |
| --- | --- |
| `{3}`, `{7}` single | correct |
| `{1,1}`, `{3,4}`, `{5,2}`, `{2,5}`, `{1,1,1}` | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| `{0,4}`, `{0,0,3}` leading empty batches | correct, they are skipped before `readRowCount` moves |
| `{4,0}` trailing empty | correct |
| `{4,0,2}` empty in the middle | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |

So the rule is: the first non-empty batch is handled correctly, and every later non-empty batch throws. It always throws, so no partially converted rows ever reach the caller on `dev` today.

### Why it has never been caught

Both tests in `ArrowToSeatunnelRowReaderTest` call `writer.writeBatch()` exactly once, `testSeatunnelRow` at `:316` and `testConvertArrowSpeed` at `:442`. A single batch makes `readRowCount` zero and `seatunnelRowBatch.size()` equal to this batch's row count, so both conventions coincide and the bug is invisible.

### A trap worth recording

The loop bound looks like the whole bug, and it is not. Correcting only the bound and leaving `readRowCount + i` on the vector removes the exception and replaces it with **silent data corruption**, because arrow returns `null` past the end instead of throwing. Measured, same 3+4 stream:

```
expected: <[0, 1, 2, 100, 101, 102, 103]>
but was:  <[0, 1, 2, 103, null, null, null]>
```

A regression test that asserts only the row count would pass against that. Any test for this needs to assert the values.

### Both halves are required

| change | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| neither (current `dev`) | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| loop bound only | no exception, wrong values as above |
| vector index only | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| both | correct |

### Fix

Bound the loop by the current batch's row count, and index the vector from 0 while continuing to index the cumulative list from `readRowCount`:

```java
for (int i = 0; i < rowCountInOneBatch; i++) {
    ...
    Object fieldValue = convertArrowData(i, minorType, fieldVector, seaTunnelDataType);
    ...
    seatunnelRowBatch.get(readRowCount + i).setField(fieldIndex, fieldValue);   // unchanged
}
```

Single-batch behaviour is unchanged by construction: with one batch `readRowCount` is 0 and `rowCountInOneBatch == seatunnelRowBatch.size()`, so both forms are identical. The existing tests, including the 1,000,000 row `testConvertArrowSpeed`, pass untouched.

Verified after the fix: all 11 shapes above return the right values in the right order, and a two-batch stream with `BIGINT`, `VARCHAR`, `ARRAY<INT>` and `TIMESTAMP` columns reads back all rows correctly, which exercises `ListConverter` and `TimeStampMilliConverter` through the changed `rowIndex`.

### Scope

`ArrowToSeatunnelRowReader` has two production callers, `DorisValueReader` and `StarRocksBeReadClient`, both passing `TScanBatchResult.getRows()` straight from the backend. As stated above, I make no claim about what those backends emit.

### SeaTunnel Version

`dev` at `11e4f5554`, 3.0.0-SNAPSHOT.

### Search before asking

- [x] Searched current issues and pull requests; related prior work is identified below.

### What happened

`RetryUtils.retryWithException` repeats an operation rejected by its retry condition when `shouldThrowException` is false. The non-retriable branch only stops in throwing mode; otherwise the loop continues and can repeat side effects. Expected: execute once and return null.

### SeaTunnel Version

dev at 11e4f5554973a66ba2d63d4df18ee22f10be121f. No claim about untested releases.

### SeaTunnel Config

Not applicable: this is the shared Java utility contract, not a connector configuration.

### Running Command

Invoke the public utility with `new RetryUtils.RetryMaterial(3, false, e -> false)` and an execution that increments an AtomicInteger then throws an IllegalStateException. After the call returns, assert the result is null and the invocation count is 1.

### Error Exception

The result is null, but the invocation count is 3 instead of 1. This is a behavioral error rather than a missing log or exception.

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Not required for the isolated utility/format reproduction.

### Java or Scala Version

JDK 17.0.18; regression cases also passed on JDK 1.8.0_492 in the original local repair batch.

### Anything else

Existing retry-related RocketMQ changes concern connector routes/IT retrying. This report is limited to the shared utility's non-throwing mode; in-tree production callers inspected use throwing mode.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR.

### Search before asking

- [x] Searched current issues and pull requests; related prior work is identified below.

### What happened

Protobuf read/write field lookup uses different case transformations. Writing an exactly named mixed-case proto field can fail after lowercasing, reading a case-variant schema field can return null, and a MAP inside a ROW is resolved against the root descriptor rather than its owning message.

### SeaTunnel Version

dev at 11e4f5554973a66ba2d63d4df18ee22f10be121f. No claim about untested releases.

### SeaTunnel Config

Minimal proto:
```proto
syntax = "proto3";
message Root {
  message Address { map<string, float> attributes = 1; }
  Address address = 1;
  string C_STRING = 2;
}
```
Use matching SeaTunnel ROW/MAP fields for address.attributes and an exact `C_STRING` schema field. Also test a scalar proto `c_string` with schema `C_String`. No broker is needed for a converter-level reproduction.

### Running Command

Construct the descriptor, serialize a SeaTunnelRow through RowToProtobufConverter, parse the bytes with DynamicMessage and read through ProtobufToRowConverter. Assert the original scalar/map values round-trip.

### Error Exception

On the baseline, exact mixed-case writes can fail in descriptor lookup, case-variant reads can yield null and nested MAP writes use a field descriptor belonging to the wrong message.

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Not required for the isolated utility/format reproduction.

### Java or Scala Version

JDK 17.0.18; regression cases also passed on JDK 1.8.0_492 in the original local repair batch.

### Anything else

Closed PR #10194 was not merged. Its review explicitly identified the remaining nested MAP descriptor problem. This report/patch continues that work with owning-message lookup and regression coverage, while retaining the case-insensitive fallback needed by existing schemas. No active equivalent PR was found.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR.

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct.

### Search before asking

- [x] Searched current issues and pull requests; related prior work is identified below.

### What happened

CSV and Text deserializers cache the timestamp formatter selected by the first row. A later supported value with a different fractional-second precision is then parsed using that stale formatter and fails.

### SeaTunnel Version

dev at 11e4f5554973a66ba2d63d4df18ee22f10be121f. No claim about untested releases.

### SeaTunnel Config

Use a two-column schema (`name` STRING, `ts` TIMESTAMP), comma delimiter, and the same deserializer instance for these successive rows:
```text
alpha,2023-01-01 00:00:00
bravo,2023-01-01 00:00:00.123
charlie,2023-01-01 00:00:00.123456
```
Repeat with TextDeserializationSchema and CsvDeserializationSchema. Reverse the precision order to exercise cache replacement in both directions.

### Running Command

Call deserialize for each row and assert the returned LocalDateTime including its nanoseconds. This reproduces the reader behavior without starting an engine.

### Error Exception

A DateTimeParseException is raised when a later value uses a different supported precision. Expected: parse every row using a matching supported pattern; unsupported text must still fail.

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Not required for the isolated utility/format reproduction.

### Java or Scala Version

JDK 17.0.18; regression cases also passed on JDK 1.8.0_492 in the original local repair batch.

### Anything else

Merged PR #11264 addressed a similar cache problem in the JSON format. CSV and Text retain the stale-formatter behavior on the current dev source and are the scope here. `timestamp_format` is a sink serialization option, not a strict source parsing pattern.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR.

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct.

## Search before asking

- [x] Searched existing issues and pull requests; no existing fix for this reproduction was found.

## What happened

DateUtils.matchDateFormatter accepts ISO local datetime text with a fractional second and optional Z, but its corresponding formatter puts the fraction and Z in the same optional block. A value such as 2024-12-16T15:33:45.123 matches the pattern and then fails to parse. This also affects DATE fields parsed from CSV/Text through DateUtils.

## SeaTunnel Version

dev at 760c33a94433db85b974ae4d6622d05b726a4a47

## SeaTunnel Config

```text
Utility-level reproduction; no job configuration required.
```

## Running Command / reproduction

Call DateUtils.parse("2024-12-16T15:33:45.123"). Expected LocalDate 2024-12-16; actual DateTimeParseException with unparsed text at index 19. The same text with a trailing Z parses. Whole-second text without Z also parses.

Regression command after adding the test:

```shell
./mvnw -q -pl seatunnel-common -am -Dtest=DateUtilsTest -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false package
```

## Error Exception

JDK 17: DateUtilsTest, 6 tests passed after the fix. Against the original formatter, the same suite produced 1 error (fractional local datetime without Z).

## Java or Scala Version

JDK 17, macOS.

## Are you willing to submit PR?

- [x] Yes

## Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow the Apache Code of Conduct.

## Search before asking

- [x] Searched existing issues and pull requests; no existing fix for this reproduction was found.

## What happened

CsvSerializationSchema joins columns with its configured delimiter but uses a comma-default CSVPrinter to decide whether each string needs quotes. With delimiter |, a value a|b is written without quotes and reads back as multiple columns.

## SeaTunnel Version

dev at 760c33a94433db85b974ae4d6622d05b726a4a47

## SeaTunnel Config

```text
field_delimiter = "|"; csv_string_quote_mode = "MINIMAL"; STRING value = "a|b"
```

## Running Command / reproduction

Serialize the row ["a|b",42,null] using delimiter="|", quoteMode=MINIMAL and nullValue="NULL", then deserialize with the same delimiter and nullFormat. Expected ["a|b",42,null]; the unpatched writer leaves the first string unquoted, so the integer column receives b or the columns shift.

Regression command after adding the test:

```shell
./mvnw -q -pl seatunnel-formats/seatunnel-format-csv -am -Dtest=CsvTextFormatSchemaTest -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false package
```

## Error Exception

JDK 17: CsvTextFormatSchemaTest, 7 tests passed after the fix. The same suite fails against the old serializer. The new container-based LocalFile scenario is separate from this unit result.

## Java or Scala Version

JDK 17, macOS.

## Are you willing to submit PR?

- [x] Yes

A streaming/batch job writing to a **multi-node IoTDB cluster (1.3.x)** dies with:

```
org.apache.iotdb.rpc.StatementExecutionException: 400:
```

### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [feature](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22Feature%22) and found no similar feature requirement.

### Description

The Zeta SQL transform does not provide `UNIX_TIMESTAMP`, a common Hive date function and the inverse of the existing `FROM_UNIXTIME`. Its absence complicates migrating Hive/Spark SQL jobs to SeaTunnel.

Proposed signatures (return `BIGINT`):

- `UNIX_TIMESTAMP()` — current epoch seconds
- `UNIX_TIMESTAMP(string[, pattern])` — parse a datetime string (default `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss`); returns NULL on parse failure, matching Hive
- `UNIX_TIMESTAMP(dateTime)` — from a LocalDateTime / OffsetDateTime / LocalDate column

### Usage Scenario

```
SELECT UNIX_TIMESTAMP(dt) FROM ...
SELECT UNIX_TIMESTAMP('2023-01-01 00:00:00')
SELECT UNIX_TIMESTAMP(s, 'yyyy/MM/dd HH:mm:ss') FROM ...
```

Today this must be rewritten with `PARSEDATETIME` plus manual epoch arithmetic.

### Related issues

None for `UNIX_TIMESTAMP`.

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://www.apache.org/foundation/policies/conduct)

### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22bug%22) and found no similar issues.

### What happened

`StringFunction.md5` only recognizes the primitive `byte[]` as binary input:

```java
// seatunnel-transforms-v2/.../StringFunction.java
public static String md5(List<Object> args) {
    ...
    if (arg instanceof byte[]) {
        return Hashing.md5().hashBytes((byte[]) arg).toString();
    }
    return Hashing.md5().hashString(arg.toString(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8).toString();
}
```

SeaTunnel array columns are **boxed** arrays at runtime: `ArrayType.BYTE_ARRAY_TYPE` is `Byte[].class` (seatunnel-api `ArrayType.java`). A `Byte[]` never matches `instanceof byte[]`, so `MD5()` applied to an `ARRAY<BYTE>` column silently falls into the `toString()` branch and hashes the JVM identity string of the array object.

Running the exact code path with the same library confirms:

```
string actually hashed            = "[Ljava.lang.Byte;@58644d46"
MD5 result run 1 (same contents)  = cceb6b971ad8573f23c3e97df9bc4ebe
MD5 result run 2 (same contents)  = e3dcfa442d03d0edc3b15b39b5144cb4
md5('hello') for reference        = 5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592
```

Two consequences:

1. The returned "MD5" has no relation to the data.
2. It is **nondeterministic** — the same input value produces a different hash on every run (identity hash code), which silently breaks any dedup/change-detection logic built on top of it.

Nothing rejects the query up front: `ZetaSQLType` infers `STRING` for `MD5(...)` without validating argument types, and `ZetaSQLFunction` passes the raw column value into the function.

`ARRAY<BYTE>` columns are produced by several connectors' type mappings (e.g. ClickHouse, Cassandra, Doris, Elasticsearch), so `SELECT MD5(arr_col)` is reachable in normal jobs.

Note that the AES functions added in the same release explicitly reject array inputs for exactly this reason — `CryptoFunction.rejectNonScalar` ("rejects array ... inputs that would otherwise be encrypted as garbage"). MD5 should apply the same guard (or handle boxed byte arrays explicitly); silently hashing the identity string is the worst possible behavior.

### SeaTunnel Version

dev (commit 0278a6a74); MD5 was added in #12564

### SeaTunnel Config

```conf
env {
  job.mode = "BATCH"
}

source {
  # any source producing an ARRAY<BYTE> column, e.g. ClickHouse `Array(Int8)`
}

transform {
  Sql {
    source_table_name = "src"
    result_table_name = "out"
    query = "SELECT MD5(arr_col) AS h FROM src"
  }
}

sink {
  Console {}
}
```

### Running Command

```shell
$SEATUNNEL_HOME/bin/seatunnel.sh --config ./md5.conf -e run
```

### Error Exception

No exception — which is the problem. The transform silently emits a 32-character hex string that (a) is not the MD5 of the data and (b) changes between runs for identical input.

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Zeta

### Java or Scala Version

Java 17

### Search before asking

- [x] I searched existing issues and PRs.

### What happened

The InfluxDB sink assigns the configured timestamp precision to values that are already epoch milliseconds. This affects both omitted `key_time` (processing time) and a `TIMESTAMP` column selected by `key_time`.

With the default nanosecond precision, `2025-01-02T03:04:05.123` becomes `1735787045123` **nanoseconds**, around 1970, instead of `1735787045123000000` nanoseconds. A seconds/minutes/hours configuration instead moves the timestamp far into the future and can exceed the server's timestamp range.

`DefaultSerializer.createTimestampExtractor` passes `System.currentTimeMillis()` and `LocalDateTime.toInstant(...).toEpochMilli()` to `Point.Builder.time(..., precision)`. The unit supplied to this builder describes the input number's unit, not the requested output precision.

### Expected behavior

Processing time and a `TIMESTAMP` value should retain their actual instant independently of `epoch`. Explicit `BIGINT` and numeric `STRING` timestamps should continue to use the configured unit.

### How to reproduce

Create a `DefaultSerializer` with row fields `time: TIMESTAMP` and `value: INT`, `key_time = "time"`, and `TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS`. Serialize a row containing `LocalDateTime.of(2025, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 123_000_000)` and `1`, then call `Point.lineProtocol()`.

```text
Actual:   metrics value=1i 1735787045123
Expected: metrics value=1i 1735787045123000000
```

The processing-time path reproduces the same unit mismatch without a `key_time` field. No running InfluxDB server is needed to inspect the generated line protocol.

### Environment and verification

Reproduced against `dev` at `b3898b62d79db47d4b213c830da8745edd8fc678`, macOS, Corretto 11.0.25, influxdb-java 2.21.

A focused regression across all six supported precisions executes 24 cases. With unchanged production code, 10 fail: processing time and `TIMESTAMP` under every non-millisecond precision. The millisecond cases and all explicit numeric/string timestamp controls pass.

Related: #12741 fixes null timestamps, retention policy and flush retries. Its serializer diff does not change either affected unit assignment. This issue tracks the separate precision correction.

### What happened

The InfluxDB sink assigns the configured timestamp precision to values that are already epoch milliseconds. This affects both omitted `key_time` (processing time) and a `TIMESTAMP` column selected by `key_time`.

With the default nanosecond precision, `2025-01-02T03:04:05.123` becomes `1735787045123` **nanoseconds**, around 1970, instead of `1735787045123000000` nanoseconds. A seconds/minutes/hours configuration instead moves the timestamp far into the future and can exceed the server's timestamp range.

`DefaultSerializer.createTimestampExtractor` passes `System.currentTimeMillis()` and `LocalDateTime.toInstant(...).toEpochMilli()` to `Point.Builder.time(..., precision)`. The unit supplied to this builder describes the input number's unit, not the requested output precision.

### Expected behavior

Processing time and a `TIMESTAMP` value should retain their actual instant independently of `epoch`. Explicit `BIGINT` and numeric `STRING` timestamps should continue to use the configured unit.

### Search before asking

I searched the open/closed Lance issues and PRs and found no report for this Map schema mismatch. #12738 addresses fragment batching, and this failure also occurs without that change.

### What happened

`FragmentConverter.writeMapToVector` rejects a valid Arrow Map field because it expects `key` and `value` to be two direct children of the Map. Arrow represents a Map with one non-null `entries` Struct child containing those two fields.

A one-row regression added to the existing `FragmentConverterTest` on current `dev` (`b0f6feddf9ed0dc1f5d485cfc69d387edfe6ac82`) fails with:

```text
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Map field must have key and value child fields
```

The existing restored-schema test passes: 2 tests run, 1 pass, 1 error. On #12738's head, both one-row and three-row Map controls fail at the same guard. The array batch control passes. This is a pre-existing Map issue, not a batching regression.

### Minimal reproduction

In `FragmentConverterTest`, construct the schema and call the existing single-row converter:

```java
SeaTunnelRowType rowType = new SeaTunnelRowType(
        new String[] {"attributes"},
        new SeaTunnelDataType<?>[] {
            new MapType<>(BasicType.STRING_TYPE, BasicType.INT_TYPE)
        });
Field entries = new Field(
        "entries",
        FieldType.notNullable(new ArrowType.Struct()),
        Arrays.asList(
                Field.notNullable("key", new ArrowType.Utf8()),
                Field.nullable("value", new ArrowType.Int(32, true))));
Schema schema = new Schema(Arrays.asList(new Field(
        "attributes",
        FieldType.nullable(new ArrowType.Map(false)),
        Arrays.asList(entries))));
try (RootAllocator allocator = new RootAllocator();
        VectorSchemaRoot root = FragmentConverter.convertToVectorSchemaRoot(
                new SeaTunnelRow(new Object[] {Map.of("a", 1)}),
                rowType, schema, allocator)) {
    Assertions.assertEquals(1, root.getRowCount());
}
```

Verified with JDK 17 and the Lance module's reactor `verify`, selecting `FragmentConverterTest`. On macOS, the test JVM arguments were overridden to `-Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED` to avoid the separate unquoted `-Dos.name=Mac OS X` launcher problem. Spotless passed; Checkstyle/license checks and live engine/Lance E2E were not run for this diagnostic.

### Expected behavior and scope

For a valid Arrow Map schema, the writer should read the key/value fields from the `entries` Struct and write the Map values. The regression should verify actual keys/values, plus empty Maps, null rows and nullable values.

There is a related schema-creation gap: current `SchemaUtils.convertSchema` constructs a Map without child fields. Supporting Map columns end to end therefore needs the schema-creation and writer paths to agree; only changing the writer guard would leave new dataset creation incomplete. I would keep this separate from #12738, preserve scalar behavior, and add EN/ZH documentation and an existing `LanceIT` scenario.

Is that the intended Map support contract for this connector? I can prepare a focused follow-up once the scope is agreed. No production fix or full job reproduction is claimed here.

### Problem

Follow-up from PR #11557 and the review discussion around Hazelcast typed reads. Two pre-existing task-operation paths do not explicitly validate the decoded wire type at the read site:

- `AssignSplitOperation#readInternal` uses `taskID = in.readObject()` without checking the decoded value is a `TaskLocation`.
- `TaskOperation#readInternal` uses `in.readObject(TaskLocation.class)`. For Hazelcast `DataSerializableSerializer`, the class argument is a construction override rather than validation of the wire factory/class id, so a mismatched payload can be consumed positionally into a new `TaskLocation`.

### Proposed scope

- Decode through the public `ObjectDataInput` contract and reject `null` or non-`TaskLocation` values at the read site with a clear `IOException`.
- Add a same-factory/different-class negative serialization test and a valid round-trip test for each path.
- Preserve the existing serializer factory IDs, class IDs, and wire format for valid payloads.

### Context

Tracked separately because both paths predate PR #11557 and are shared by legacy task operations. Review context: https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/pull/11557#issuecomment-6008751359

### Search before asking

- [x] Searched existing issues and PRs. #12685 identifies this as the separate realtime follow-up; #12688 implements its checkpoint-history slice. No separate CLI realtime-diagnosis PR was found. #11352 covers the dedicated UI, which remains separate.

### Description

Extend `seatunnel --diagnose <jobId>` with evidence from retained realtime edge/vertex metrics. Checkpoint history can explain that a running job degraded, but cannot identify which queue/downstream vertex is under sustained pressure.

The output identifies a **candidate to investigate**, retaining queue ID, target vertex, measured window and ratios. A source's read time alone must not blame the source, because it can include synchronous downstream work. Sink prepare/commit time remains visible when write busyness is low.

DanielLeens confirmed the read-only evidence scope [in this discussion](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues/12750#issuecomment-6145194685). The first PR will wait for #12631/#12688 to merge, then rebase onto current `dev`, excluding their pending changes.

A working prototype is available on [feat/realtime-cli-prototype](https://github.com/CryoThrust/seatunnel/tree/feat/realtime-cli-prototype). Its integration base `210e7eb191e36e190cc51f8014bb86edf50c73c4` combines `dev` at `b0f6fedd` with the still-open parent changes, preserving their authorship. The [six-file follow-up comparison](https://github.com/CryoThrust/seatunnel/compare/210e7eb191e36e190cc51f8014bb86edf50c73c4...feat/realtime-cli-prototype) contains only this follow-up. It is not a ready-to-merge PR.

Initial rules:

- Match the endpoints' window intersection, bucket width, timestamps and target vertex. Require the latest three completed buckets in that shared engine window. Preserve individual queues; exclude partial/conflicting points. Missing recent buckets cannot be replaced by an older matched run.
- Report persistent queue pressure when all three buckets have `bpRatio >= 0.5` and `queueFillRatio >= 0.8`. Busy downstream sink writes/transform processing provide corroboration, not root-cause proof. Preserve raw backpressure ratios, including values above one.
- Analyze `(sinkPrepareCommitNs + sinkCommitNs) / (bucketNs * subtaskCount)` separately, with the same persistence requirement and an initial 0.5 threshold.
- Missing/disabled/insufficient evidence is a coverage gap, including a missing queue next to a healthy one. Optional metric failures preserve job/checkpoint diagnosis; only running jobs request realtime data.

### Usage Scenario

A CDC job remains RUNNING with both counters advancing, but its lag grows. With `env.engine.observability.enabled = true`, read-only diagnosis correlates a full/backpressured queue with work in its downstream vertex, or explains that available metrics cannot establish the cause. No provider/API key is needed.

### Output example

Rendered by the actual `--diagnose` command against loopback HTTP fixtures; timestamps are synthetic milliseconds, not a live-cluster measurement. The prototype now exposes `bucketMs` as requested. Queue -3 targets vertex 1 over three completed five-second buckets; the vertex is a candidate to investigate, not a root-cause conclusion.

```text
Job 852 (unnamed) — RUNNING
  [warning] Queue -3 into vertex 1 was persistently backpressured in the matched window. Downstream sink
writes were busy too; investigate this vertex as a bottleneck candidate. (queueId=-3 targetVertexId=1
buckets=3 window=0..15000ms bucketMs=5000 median bpRatio=0.80 queueFillRatio=0.90)
```

Disabled observability gives a coverage gap:

```text
Job 852 (unnamed) — RUNNING
  [info] Realtime pressure checks unavailable: engine.observability.enabled is false.
```

### Verification

Python 3.10 and 3.13 each pass the complete CLI suite: 380 tests plus three subtests, zero failures/errors/skips. Ruff passes. Loopback HTTP tests exercise actual GET paths, terminal rendering, model-free execution and optional endpoint failure.

Fixtures cover transient/sustained pressure, missing/conflicting buckets, disabled metrics, multiple queues sharing a target, an empty upstream queue, source-read non-attribution, commit-only sink work, and boundary/window alignment. The recent-gap controls fail six cases on the earlier prototype: it falls back to older pressure/commit samples or reports no finding for stale healthy samples. The corrected window selection passes them, with two additional HTTP CLI controls.

```sh
cd seatunnel-cli
python -m pytest tests -q
ruff check .
```

English/Chinese CLI docs are included. Root-only Maven formatting and skip-tests verification pass; no full Zeta build or live cluster verification is claimed. No generation benchmark improvement is expected from a model-free diagnosis branch.

### Related issues

#12685, #12688, #12631, #12630. This does not take over #11352.

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [x] Yes, after the parent diagnosis changes merge, with the agreed scope and a current-dev rebase.

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct.

### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22bug%22) and found no similar issues.

### What happened

The Doris connector maps `LARGEINT` to `DecimalType(20, 0)` (`AbstractDorisTypeConverter#convert`). Doris `LARGEINT` is a 128-bit signed integer, so its values range from -2^127 to 2^127-1, which is up to 39 digits. The declared precision of 20 is too small.

The source reader itself returns the full value; only the declared schema is wrong. Any downstream that trusts the schema therefore creates a column that is too narrow. When a value with more than 20 digits arrives, the job fails.

I reproduced this end to end with the **3.0.0 release** against **Doris 4.0.6**. The mapping code is unchanged since #6354, so `dev` behaves the same. The source table has 5 rows:

| id | value | digits |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 12345 | 5 |
| 2 | 99999999999999999999 | 20 |
| 3 | 100000000000000000000 | 21 |
| 4 | 170141183460469231731687303715884105727 (max) | 39 |
| 5 | -170141183460469231731687303715884105728 (min) | 39 + sign |

| Job | Result |
|---|---|
| Doris → Console | All 5 values printed intact. The reader is fine. |
| Doris → Doris, auto-create | OK. `reconvert()` special-cases `sourceType = largeint` and recreates a `largeint` column. |
| **Doris → MySQL 8 (JDBC), auto-create** | Target column created as **`decimal(20,0)`**. The job fails on row 3: `Out of range value for column 'v'`, and 0 rows are written. Non-strict `sql_mode` fails the same way, because Connector/J reports the truncation. |

Doris → Doris only works because of the `sourceType` special case in `reconvert()`. Every other sink gets `DECIMAL(20,0)`. `ARRAY<largeint>` has the same problem (`DorisTypeConverterV2`, `new DecimalArrayType(new DecimalType(20, 0))`). `MAX_DORIS_LARGEINT_TO_VARCHAR_LENGTH = 39` is defined in the converter but is not used.

**Fix options.** The full `LARGEINT` range needs 39 digits. `DecimalType` itself has no cap, but sink converters do: `MySqlTypeConverter.MAX_PRECISION = 65`, whereas Doris and Oracle cap at 38.
1. Map to `DECIMAL(39,0)`. This is exact and keeps the numeric type. Sinks that allow 39 digits, such as MySQL, are correct. How sinks capped at 38 handle a 39-digit decimal still needs checking for each one.
2. Map to `STRING` with length 39. This is lossless everywhere, but downstream gets a string column instead of a number.

Either way, the existing `sourceType = largeint` special case for Doris → Doris would stay. I lean towards option 1, since it fixes the reproduced failure without changing the logical type, but I'd appreciate a maintainer's preference before I open a PR.

3.0.0 (also present on dev)

### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [feature](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22Feature%22) and found no similar feature requirement.

### Description

`CheckpointMonitorService` is constructed with a hardcoded history size in `SeaTunnelServer.startMaster()`:

```java
checkpointMonitorService = new CheckpointMonitorService(engineContext, 32);
```

That 32 is how many completed checkpoints the monitor keeps **per pipeline** for the `/jobs/checkpoints/{jobId}` endpoint (`PipelineCheckpointOverview.addHistory` trims to it). There is no configuration option for it, so an operator cannot change the retained window.

### Why it matters

The window bounds how far back a client can compare a job against its own past, which is what diagnosing a *gradual* slowdown needs — the case where a job is still `RUNNING`, both row counters are moving, `restoreCount` is 0, and the only evidence that anything changed is that checkpoints now take longer than they used to.

How much history 32 entries buys depends entirely on the checkpoint interval, and the mismatch is large:

| `checkpoint.interval` | history covered by 32 entries |
|---|---|
| 300000 ms (engine default) | ~2.5 hours |
| 60000 ms | ~32 minutes |
| 10000 ms (common for CDC) | **~5 minutes** |

Five minutes of baseline is not enough to distinguish a trend from noise, and a short interval is exactly what a latency-sensitive CDC job is configured with. The trend rules added in #12688 consume this endpoint and are limited by it; the `seatunnel-cli` README has to tell users the window is 32 checkpoints because there is nothing they can do about it.

### Proposal

Add `seatunnel.engine.checkpoint.monitor-history-size`, defaulting to 32 so current behaviour is unchanged:

```yaml
seatunnel:
  engine:
    checkpoint:
      monitor-history-size: 128
```

The history is retained in memory per pipeline, so a larger window costs memory proportional to the number of running pipelines; that trade-off belongs in the documentation rather than in a hidden constant.

### Usage Scenario

A CDC job with `checkpoint.interval = 10000` that degrades over an hour. With the current fixed window the retained history only reaches back about five minutes, so by the time someone looks, the comparison that would show the degradation has already rolled out of the window. Raising the size to 128 covers roughly 20 minutes at that interval.

### Related issues

- #12688 — the checkpoint trend rules that read this endpoint

- [X] I had searched in the [feature](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22Feature%22) and found no similar feature requirement.

### Description

`CheckpointMonitorService` is constructed with a hardcoded history size in `SeaTunnelServer.startMaster()`:

```java
checkpointMonitorService = new CheckpointMonitorService(engineContext, 32);
```

That 32 is how many completed checkpoints the monitor keeps **per pipeline** for the `/jobs/checkpoints/{jobId}` endpoint (`PipelineCheckpointOverview.addHistory` trims to it). There is no configuration option for it, so an operator cannot change the retained window.

### Why it matters

The window bounds how far back a client can compare a job against its own past, which is what diagnosing a *gradual* slowdown needs — the case where a job is still `RUNNING`, both row counters are moving, `restoreCount` is 0, and the only evidence that anything changed is that checkpoints now take longer than they used to.

How much history 32 entries buys depends entirely on the checkpoint interval, and the mismatch is large:

| `checkpoint.interval` | history covered by 32 entries |
|---|---|
| 300000 ms (engine default) | ~2.5 hours |
| 60000 ms | ~32 minutes |
| 10000 ms (common for CDC) | **~5 minutes** |

Five minutes of baseline is not enough to distinguish a trend from noise, and a short interval is exactly what a latency-sensitive CDC job is configured with. The trend rules added in #12688 consume this endpoint and are limited by it; the `seatunnel-cli` README has to tell users the window is 32 checkpoints because there is nothing they can do about it.

### Proposal

Add `seatunnel.engine.checkpoint.monitor-history-size`, defaulting to 32 so current behaviour is unchanged:

```yaml
seatunnel:
  engine:
    checkpoint:
      monitor-history-size: 128
```

The history is retained in memory per pipeline, so a larger window costs memory proportional to the number of running pipelines; that trade-off belongs in the documentation rather than in a hidden constant.

### Usage Scenario

A CDC job with `checkpoint.interval = 10000` that degrades over an hour. With the current fixed window the retained history only reaches back about five minutes, so by the time someone looks, the comparison that would show the degradation has already rolled out of the window. Raising the size to 128 covers roughly 20 minutes at that interval.

- #12688 — the checkpoint trend rules that read this endpoint

### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [feature](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22Feature%22) and found no similar feature requirement.

### Description

`GET /jobs/checkpoints/{jobId}` returns no response timestamp, so a client cannot work out how long an `inProgress` checkpoint has been running from the response alone.

The response has `updatedAt`, which looks like it would serve and does not. The engine sets it inside `HazelcastCheckpointOverviewStateStore.updateOverview`:

```java
updater.accept(pipeline);
snapshot.setUpdatedAt(System.currentTimeMillis());
```

That callback runs only when a checkpoint *event* is recorded — `CheckpointMonitorService` calls it on trigger, acknowledge, complete, fail and restore. While a checkpoint hangs waiting for its last subtask, nothing is written, so the newest write is that final acknowledgement a few seconds after the trigger. `updatedAt - triggerTimestamp` therefore freezes at a few seconds and never grows, and a hung barrier is invisible to any client that ages a checkpoint that way.

Today's documentation describes the field as "Latest snapshot timestamp (millisecond)", which does not convey that.

### Why it matters

Ageing an in-progress checkpoint is the main thing a client wants from this endpoint, and the only clock currently available is the client's own. That is wrong in both directions: a client whose clock runs ahead of the cluster invents stalls, and one running behind hides them.

The workaround available today is to call `/job-info/{jobId}` as well and borrow `diagnostics.generatedAt` from it, which `JobRuntimeDiagnostics.build` does stamp at response time. That is what the `--diagnose` rules in #12688 ended up doing. It works, but it means a client that only cares about checkpoints has to fetch an unrelated endpoint to get a clock, and it is fragile: the `diagnostics` block is only present while the master can serve it.

### Proposal

Add `generatedAt` to the response, stamped while it is built, mirroring what `/job-info` already does for its `diagnostics` block:

```json
{
  "jobId": "1234567890",
  "generatedAt": 1720000006500,
  "updatedAt": 1720000000123,
  "pipelines": [ ... ]
}
```

Additive, so no existing client is affected. Worth adding before the overview lookup so it is present even when there is nothing to report — the monitor service being off, or nothing recorded for the job yet — which is precisely when a client wants to know the answer came from a live server rather than a cache.

The documentation for `updatedAt` should also say what it actually is, so the next reader does not make the same inference from the field name.

### Usage Scenario

A client polling `/jobs/checkpoints/{jobId}` to answer "is a checkpoint stuck?": it reads `inProgress[].triggerTimestamp` and needs a trustworthy "now" from the same response to subtract it from.

### Related issues

- #12688 — the checkpoint rules that needed this and had to borrow the clock from `/job-info`

### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the issues and found no similar issues.

### What happened

DECIMAL and DOUBLE values lose precision in an Excel round trip (file sink `file_format_type = "excel"`, then file source reading the same files).

Write side, `ExcelGenerator#setCellValue`:

```java
case DECIMAL:
    cell.setCellValue(Double.parseDouble(value.toString()));
```

A `DECIMAL(20, 4)` value is converted to `double`, so anything beyond about 15-17 significant digits is lost before it reaches the file.

Read side, `ExcelReadStrategy#getCellValue` (POI path for `.xlsx` / `.xls`):

```java
case NUMERIC:
    ...
    return formatter.formatCellValue(cell);
```

`DataFormatter` renders the cell with the "General" style, which keeps only about 10 significant digits. The source then parses that string, so DOUBLE and DECIMAL values are truncated even when the file itself holds the full `double` value. `ExcelCellUtils#convert` also builds decimals through `BigDecimal.valueOf(Double.parseDouble(...))`.

### How to reproduce (verified on `dev` 42d2aab)

Round trip of 3000 rows: MySQL `DECIMAL(20,4)` / `DOUBLE` -> LocalFile excel -> LocalFile excel source -> MySQL, compared column by column:

| column  | mismatched rows (of 3000) | example (source -> after round trip) |
|---------|---------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| DOUBLE  | 2512 | `10.285714285` -> `10.28571428` |
| DECIMAL | 2241 | `1012345.6699` -> `1012345.6700` |

The same pipeline with csv, text, json, parquet and orc has 0 mismatches.

### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22bug%22) and found no similar issues.

### What happened

Restoring a Zeta job whose JDBC sink runs with `is_exactly_once = true` fails whenever the restored checkpoint's XA transactions were already committed, which is the normal case after a failure.

On restore, `SinkAggregatedCommitterTask.restoreState` calls `restoreCommit` on the sink's aggregated committer. Every sink runs inside `MultiTableSink`, so that is `MultiTableSinkAggregatedCommitter`. It does not override `restoreCommit`, so the interface default calls `commit()`, which calls each table's `commit()`, never its `restoreCommit()`.

`JdbcSinkAggregatedCommitter.restoreCommit` (#11569) skips transactions that are no longer prepared. Because it is never reached, the restore commits the checkpoint's XIDs again, MySQL answers `XAER_NOTA`, the commit failure propagates, and the job fails to restore.

Reproduced end to end on a 2.3.12-based build with #11569 and #10459 backported; `MultiTableSinkAggregatedCommitter` on dev is unchanged, so dev takes the same path (MySQL-CDC → JDBC, MySQL 8.4):
1. Run a streaming job with the config below and let a few checkpoints complete.
2. Fail the job, for example a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger on the target that raises an error.
3. Remove the cause and restore: `seatunnel.sh -r <jobId> -c job.conf`.
4. The restore fails every time.

### SeaTunnel Version

dev (c37823b9a); reproduced on 2.3.12 + #11569/#10459

### SeaTunnel Config

```conf
env { parallelism = 1, job.mode = "STREAMING", checkpoint.interval = 5000 }
source {
  MySQL-CDC {
    base-url = "jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/s"
    username = "root", password = "pw"
    database-names = ["s"]
    table-pattern = "s\\.t[123]"
    startup.mode = "latest"
  }
}
sink {
  Jdbc {
    url = "jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/m3"
    driver = "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver"
    username = "st", password = "stpw"
    database = "m3"
    table = "${table_name}"
    generate_sink_sql = true
    is_exactly_once = true
    xa_data_source_class_name = "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.MysqlXADataSource"
  }
}
```

### Running Command

```shell
./bin/seatunnel.sh -c job.conf --async
./bin/seatunnel.sh -r <jobId> -c job.conf --async
```

### Error Exception

```log
JdbcConnectorException: ErrorCode:[JDBC-03], ErrorDescription:[Xa operation failed, such as (commit, rollback) etc..] - unable to commit XA transaction, xid: 201:..., error -4: Xid is not valid. [XAER_NOTA: Unknown XID]
```

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Zeta

### Java or Scala Version

1.8

### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22bug%22) and found no similar issues.

### What happened

With `enable_upsert = false`, the JDBC sink silently drops a row that is inserted and then updated within the same flush.

`BufferReducedBatchStatementExecutor` keeps only the last change per primary key. For an `INSERT` followed by an `UPDATE_AFTER` of the same key, the buffer keeps the `UPDATE_AFTER`. `InsertOrUpdateBatchStatementExecutor` then picks the statement from the row kind, so it runs `UPDATE ... WHERE pk = ?` against a row that does not exist yet: 0 rows are affected, the row is never inserted, and no error is raised. Later updates of that row are lost the same way.

The reverse case breaks too: a `DELETE` followed by an `INSERT` of the same key is reduced to an `INSERT` of a row that is still in the table, which fails with a duplicate key.

With `is_exactly_once = true`, the buffer is flushed only at each checkpoint, so every row created and changed within one checkpoint interval is lost.

Reproduced end to end on 2.3.12; `BufferReducedBatchStatementExecutor.addToBatch` and `InsertOrUpdateBatchStatementExecutor.existRow` are the same on dev (MySQL-CDC → JDBC, MySQL 8.4, config below):

```sql
INSERT INTO s.t1 VALUES (99001, ...); UPDATE s.t1 SET amount = 2 WHERE id = 99001;  -- same flush: row never reaches the target
INSERT INTO s.t1 VALUES (99002, ...);  -- wait for a checkpoint
UPDATE s.t1 SET amount = 2 WHERE id = 99002;  -- next flush: correct
```

Under a mixed insert/update load on 8 tables (about 2,600 operations), 50 of 960 rows were missing from the target with no restarts at all.

### SeaTunnel Version

2.3.12 and dev (c37823b9a)

### SeaTunnel Config

```conf
sink {
  Jdbc {
    url = "jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/m3"
    driver = "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver"
    username = "st", password = "stpw"
    database = "m3"
    table = "${table_name}"
    generate_sink_sql = true
    enable_upsert = false
  }
}
```

### Running Command

```shell
./bin/seatunnel.sh -c job.conf --async
```

### Error Exception

```log
No exception. The row is missing from the target table.
```

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Zeta

### Java or Scala Version

1.8

### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [feature](https://github.com/apache/seatunnel/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22Feature%22) and found no similar feature requirement.


### Description

SeaTunnel currently lacks end-to-end support for synchronizing MySQL spatial columns to OpenSearch.
We would like to support the following data path:
```text
MySQL spatial columns
→ MySQL-CDC / Debezium
→ SeaTunnel
→ Elasticsearch/OpenSearch sink
```
The feature should support MySQL spatial types including:
- `GEOMETRY`
- `POINT`
- `LINESTRING`
- `POLYGON`
- `MULTIPOINT`
- `MULTILINESTRING`
- `MULTIPOLYGON`
- `GEOMETRYCOLLECTION`

MySQL-CDC should preserve the spatial value, spatial type, and SRID during both the initial snapshot and incremental binlog phases. SeaTunnel should retain these spatial semantics through the pipeline instead of treating the value as ordinary binary data.

### OpenSearch type mapping
OpenSearch represents geographic data using `geo_point` and `geo_shape`. The expected mapping is:
- MySQL `POINT` → OpenSearch `geo_point`
- Other MySQL spatial types → OpenSearch `geo_shape`
### SRID handling
MySQL spatial values can use different valid SRIDs. MySQL-CDC and its underlying Debezium data path should preserve any MySQL-valid SRID without restricting it based on the target system.
The source and sink responsibilities should be clearly separated:
- MySQL-CDC and Debezium should preserve the original geometry value and any valid source SRID.
- SeaTunnel should carry the geometry and SRID through the pipeline without silently transforming or discarding the spatial reference information.
- The SRID restriction applies only when writing to OpenSearch.
- OpenSearch `geo_point` and `geo_shape` do not store an SRID and interpret geographic coordinates as WGS84 longitude and latitude.
- Spatial values with SRID `4326` can therefore be written directly to OpenSearch.
- Spatial values with another SRID must not be silently interpreted as WGS84. They should either be explicitly transformed to WGS84 before reaching the sink or be rejected by the OpenSearch sink with a clear error.
The internal representation, validation stage, and possible coordinate transformation mechanism can be discussed in the implementation PR.


### Usage Scenario

Applications commonly store locations, routes, areas, and geofences in MySQL spatial columns.
Users need MySQL-CDC to synchronize both existing data and subsequent binlog changes to OpenSearch for location-based search, proximity search, and spatial relationship queries.

### Related issues

There was a previously closed issue, #8548, which attempted to convert MySQL geometry values emitted by Debezium into the existing SeaTunnel `BYTES` type.
It did not introduce spatial types in SeaTunnel or support synchronizing spatial data to OpenSearch `geo_point` and `geo_shape` fields. Therefore, it does not cover the feature requested in this issue.

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://www.apache.org/foundation/policies/conduct)

body_text:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched existing issues and open/closed PRs for this objective and did not find a matching fix.

### What happened

Avro, ordinary JSON, CSV, Text and ordinary Protobuf deserializers, plus the native and compatible Kafka Connect readers stamp a configured catalog table's path into `SeaTunnelRow.tableId` using `Optional<TablePath>.toString()`. This produces `Optional[database.schema.table]` rather than the table identifier `database.schema.table`.

The data fields deserialize successfully, so the malformed metadata can reach downstream consumers. Writers that look up or route by tableId can receive a different key from the catalog table's path. This report concerns the returned metadata; removing the wrapper alone does not change a connector's routing priority or guarantee that every flat Pulsar pipeline routes to its configured sink topic.

I reproduced the same assertion failure in the five ordinary formats using real serialized payloads, and in Kafka Connect native records, compatible object payloads and compatible array payloads using real ConsumerRecord and JsonConverter instances. The JSON reproduction uses `collect(byte[], Collector)`, which is the path that stamps its metadata. Three controls without a catalog table (JSON, CSV and Text) retain the expected empty tableId; null ConsumerRecord inputs also emit no rows.

### SeaTunnel Version

Current `dev`, commit `e2957d27afa29d4de4324cf642450757d865b902` (3.0.1-SNAPSHOT).

### SeaTunnel Config

This is reproducible directly through the format API without a job configuration. For example, add this case to the existing `AvroSerializationSchemaTest`:

```java
@Test
public void testPlainTableId() throws IOException {
    SeaTunnelRowType rowType = new SeaTunnelRowType(
            new String[] {"id"},
            new SeaTunnelDataType<?>[] {BasicType.INT_TYPE});
    CatalogTable table = CatalogTableUtil.getCatalogTable(
            "catalog", "database", "schema", "table", rowType);
    byte[] bytes = new AvroSerializationSchema(rowType)
            .serialize(new SeaTunnelRow(new Object[] {7}));
    SeaTunnelRow row = new AvroDeserializationSchema(table).deserialize(bytes);
    Assertions.assertEquals(table.getTablePath().toString(), row.getTableId());
}
```

### Running Command

```sh
./mvnw -B -pl seatunnel-formats/seatunnel-format-avro -am -Dtest=AvroSerializationSchemaTest#testPlainTableId -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false package
```

### Error Exception

The expected value is `database.schema.table`; the actual value is `Optional[database.schema.table]`.

Across the targeted baseline runs, 12 tests executed: 8 metadata assertion failures, 4 passing controls, 0 errors and 0 skips. The original five-format run contributed 5 failures and 3 no-catalog controls; Kafka Connect added failures for native records, object payloads and array payloads plus a passing null-record control. Avro/JSON/CSV/Text ran on JDK 17; Protobuf ran on Linux x86_64/JDK 17 to avoid the separate macOS ARM compiler issue #12897. No production source was changed for these reproductions.

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Not needed for the direct API reproduction.

### Java or Scala Version

JDK 17.

### Screenshots

Not applicable.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

Yes, I am preparing a focused fix that unwraps the `TablePath`, preserves no-catalog behavior and payload values, and adds regressions for all seven deserializers plus EN/ZH compatibility notes. Connector routing policy and Avro wire-layout changes are outside this fix.

AI assistance was used for investigation and test drafting; the reported reproductions were executed.

### Search before asking

- [x] I searched issues and open/closed PRs for this converter and ByteBuffer handling and found no matching fix.

### What happened

`AvroToRowConverter` converts an Avro `bytes` value using `ByteBuffer.array()`. That returns the backing allocation rather than the logical bytes between `position` and `limit`. A bounded or sliced heap buffer therefore includes unrelated bytes; direct and read-only buffers throw exceptions.

This also reproduces with a real Avro reader reusing a record: read a 64-byte value, then reuse the record for a 3-byte value. The buffer retains its larger capacity, and the public converter returns 64 bytes instead of 3.

The scope is the public `converter(GenericRecord, SeaTunnelRowType)` and `getReader()` APIs. The current Kafka/Pulsar `AvroDeserializationSchema` path calls `read(null, ...)`, so it does not take the record-reuse path. I am not claiming that normal connector payloads currently hit this failure.

### SeaTunnel Version

Current `dev`, commit `e2957d27afa29d4de4324cf642450757d865b902` (3.0.1-SNAPSHOT).

### SeaTunnel Config

Direct converter API reproduction, with the real `BYTES` type (`PrimitiveByteArrayType.INSTANCE`):

```java
SeaTunnelRowType type = new SeaTunnelRowType(
        new String[] {"bytes"},
        new SeaTunnelDataType<?>[] {PrimitiveByteArrayType.INSTANCE});
AvroSerializationSchema serializer = new AvroSerializationSchema(type);
AvroToRowConverter converter = new AvroToRowConverter(type);
DatumReader<GenericRecord> reader = converter.getReader();
byte[] first = serializer.serialize(new SeaTunnelRow(new Object[] {new byte[64]}));
byte[] second = serializer.serialize(new SeaTunnelRow(new Object[] {new byte[] {1, 2, 3}}));
GenericRecord oldRecord = reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(first, null));
GenericRecord reused = reader.read(oldRecord, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(second, null));
SeaTunnelRow row = converter.converter(reused, type);
Assertions.assertArrayEquals(new byte[] {1, 2, 3}, (byte[]) row.getField(0));
```

### Running Command

I added regressions to the existing `AvroConverterTest` and ran:

```sh
./mvnw -B -pl seatunnel-formats/seatunnel-format-avro -am -Dtest=AvroConverterTest -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false package
```

### Error Exception

10 executed tests: 3 assertion failures (bounded heap, sliced heap, real reader reuse), 2 errors (`UnsupportedOperationException` for a direct buffer and `ReadOnlyBufferException` for a read-only buffer), 0 skips. The ordinary heap, empty, null and normal serialization/deserialization controls passed, as did the existing converter test.

The record-reuse assertion expected 3 bytes but received 64. No production source was modified for these reproductions.

### Zeta or Flink or Spark Version

Not needed for the direct API reproduction.

### Java or Scala Version

JDK 17.

### Screenshots

Not applicable.

### Are you willing to submit PR?

Yes. I plan to read only the buffer's remaining region without changing its position or limit, preserve the existing full-array fast path used by normal connector reads, and keep the regressions in the existing test class. No configuration or Avro wire-layout change is intended.

AI assistance was used for investigation and test drafting; the reported failures and controls were actually executed.

### Search before asking

- [x] I searched existing issues and PRs for Avro schema caching and `RowToAvroConverter`. #11660 concerns the Parquet data model; this follow-up concerns nested ROW conversion in `seatunnel-format-avro`.

### Description

Track the non-blocking performance follow-up requested in the review of #12900.

In `RowToAvroConverter.resolveObject`, each non-null ROW calls the schema converter before creating its `GenericRecordBuilder`. This rebuilds a schema tree for each nested ROW value, including ROWs inside ARRAYs and MAPs. The legacy path already has this behavior; the nullable-layout option in #12900 is not its origin.

The goal is to reuse immutable nested schemas without changing serialized bytes or record names. No allocation benchmark has been run for this issue, so there is no measured performance claim yet.

A follow-up should preserve:

- Default and explicit `avro_row_nullable = false` bytes and legacy nested record names.
- Nullable union layout and resolution of present and null ROWs at every depth.
- Different ROW structures with the same leaf name under different parents; a cache keyed only by field name would conflate them.
- Public serializer/deserializer behavior and Kafka/Pulsar option wiring.

Before choosing a cache or reusing branches of the enclosing schema, compare allocation profiles and run the existing byte-compatibility and nested round-trip regressions. This issue tracks that investigation separately from the correctness fix in #12900.

### Usage Scenario

Avro serialization of rows containing nested ROW fields, including ROW elements in ARRAYs and MAP values, as used by Kafka and Pulsar jobs.

### Related issues

#12879, #12900

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [x] Yes. I can investigate this as a separate follow-up after the current correctness changes.

body_text:
## Bug description

During Zeta fixed-slot scheduling and failover convergence, a multi-slot request can partially succeed before another slot request fails. The current request path completes the allocation failure before asynchronous rollback finishes. A later retry can then race with slots that are still owned by the failed request.

The same failure chain exposes several related state inconsistencies:

- missing-slot retries compress request indexes and can overwrite previously allocated non-contiguous slots;
- a resource that fails fixed-worker pre-check is not reliably carried into dynamic-worker fallback;
- synchronous slot-release failures can escape the rollback future and leave the outer request unresolved;
- failed task deployment can transiently publish RUNNING, and the pipeline can publish RUNNING without checking every vertex result;
- null, exceptional, or cancelled slot futures can bypass complete cleanup bookkeeping;
- querying job status during the live-to-history convergence window can dereference a missing historical state.

## Expected behavior

- Preserve each original request index through fixed and dynamic allocation attempts.
- Complete a failed allocation only after bounded rollback attempts finish, and retain rollback failure as diagnostic context.
- Retry only releases that have not already succeeded.
- Publish task and pipeline RUNNING states only after successful deployment, while accepting vertices that have already finished normally.
- Treat null, exceptional, and cancelled slot futures as missing allocations while retaining successfully owned slots for cleanup.
- Return UNKNOWABLE when neither live nor historical job status is available.

## Scope

This issue does not include the stale-slot pipeline restore problem tracked by #12509 and addressed by #12510. It also does not include the CDC acknowledgement chain in #12163 or the idle-reader checkpoint recovery in #12388.

## Question

I maintain RouteContract, a test-only execution-contract library pinned to ShardingSphere-JDBC 5.5.3. I would like to clarify the supported boundary for an external `SQLExecutionHook` provider:

1. Is classpath registration through `META-INF/services/org.apache.shardingsphere.infra.executor.sql.hook.SQLExecutionHook` intended for external test providers? May a provider rely on a fresh instance per physical execution attempt and the same instance receiving `start` and the normal-success terminal, allowing object-local correlation? Or are these internal implementation details?
2. What compatibility expectations should a version-pinned observer have when upgrading ShardingSphere? If another documented extension point is preferred, which one?

### Reproduction and scope

[Standalone runnable probe, pinned revision](https://gist.github.com/ym0506/3d03a9d5d158c52a6a2a1848605f779b/a5b99236810f44ded981b6f340a4623345ef8fd8): Java 17, exact ShardingSphere 5.5.3, disposable MySQL containers, synchronous non-batch `PreparedStatement` reads. No RouteContract dependency, Java agent, or patched upstream classes.

After one unobserved warm-up, two equality reads and one fan-out read return the same complete synthetic row. Four start/success pairs occur on four distinct used provider objects, with no reuse or unmatched terminal. The observer ignores hook arguments. Three JUnit tests pass: one native MySQL test and two manually invoked recorder controls. A second run from the portable bundle produces the same result; both runs are my own verification. The README and POM state the exact dependencies and limitations.

This agrees with the 5.5.3 implementation in [JDBCExecutorCallback](https://github.com/apache/shardingsphere/blob/8d35894433416ef249ebb6ea21f8a8749648e9b6/infra/executor/src/main/java/org/apache/shardingsphere/infra/executor/sql/execute/engine/driver/jdbc/JDBCExecutorCallback.java#L78-L104), [SPISQLExecutionHook](https://github.com/apache/shardingsphere/blob/8d35894433416ef249ebb6ea21f8a8749648e9b6/infra/executor/src/main/java/org/apache/shardingsphere/infra/executor/sql/hook/SPISQLExecutionHook.java#L29-L45), and [RegisteredShardingSphereSPI](https://github.com/apache/shardingsphere/blob/8d35894433416ef249ebb6ea21f8a8749648e9b6/infra/spi/src/main/java/org/apache/shardingsphere/infra/spi/RegisteredShardingSphereSPI.java#L58-L68). Passing tests do not establish a supported contract; that is what I am asking about.

I searched the documentation and open/closed issues, including #26323 and the former SPI-document removal in #27596, but could not find an explicit answer. Exceptional terminal delivery in #39763 is separate and excluded here, as are batches, forced callback overlap, and arbitrary asynchronous application work.

Codex materially assisted the investigation, reproducer, and write-up. Thank you for guidance on the intended boundary.
